One scale per row confines the damage to the row that holds the outlier and cuts the mean error to 0.005; the two rows without it, quantised on their own, are off by only 0.00005. This is the whole story of modern quantisation in one test: outliers are the enemy, and the answer is smaller groups (per channel, or blocks of 32 to 128 values as in GPTQ, AWQ and the GGUF formats used by llama.cpp) or handling the outliers separately (LLM.int8()). QLoRA goes further, to 4 bits with a number format shaped for normally distributed weights.

exercises.title: Speculative decoding
exercises.statement:
A small draft model proposes several tokens quickly; the large target model checks them all in one pass. A drafted token is accepted with probability min(1, p / q), where p is the target's probability for that token and q the draft's.

Write two functions.

  • accepted(q_probs, p_probs, uniforms): the three lists give, for each drafted token in order, the draft's probability, the target's probability and a random number between 0 and 1. Token i is accepted if uniforms[i] < min(1, p_probs[i] / q_probs[i]). Stop at the first rejection. Return how many tokens were accepted.
  • residual(p, q): when a token is rejected, the target samples a replacement from max(0, p_j - q_j) for every token j, divided by the total. p and q are full distributions (lists). If every difference is 0, return p unchanged.
hints: For each drafted token, work out the acceptance threshold min(1, p / q) and compare the random number with it.
When the target likes a token at least as much as the draft (p >= q), it is always accepted. Count until the first rejection and stop.
residual: r = [max(0.0, a - b) for a, b in zip(p, q)], total = sum(r), then return p if total == 0 else [v / total for v in r].
exercises.explanation: The acceptance rule plus sampling a rejected token from the residual makes the output follow the target model's distribution exactly; this is the result of Leviathan et al. (2023). The speed-up comes from checking k drafted tokens in one forward pass of the large model, which costs about as much as generating one token, because decoding is limited by memory reads rather than arithmetic. If the draft agrees with the target often, several tokens arrive per pass; if it rarely agrees, the drafting is wasted. Medusa and EAGLE replace the separate draft model with extra heads on the target itself.

exercises.title: Cutting documents into chunks
exercises.statement:
Before a document can be searched it is cut into chunks. Chunks that overlap keep a sentence that falls on a boundary whole in at least one of them.

Write chunk_words(text, size, overlap). Split text into words on whitespace. Each chunk is size words joined by single spaces; each chunk starts size - overlap words after the previous one. Stop after the first chunk that reaches the last word. Return the list of chunks (an empty list for empty text). Raise ValueError if overlap is not smaller than size.

tests.test: print(chunk_words('a b c d e f g h i j', 4, 1))
tests.expected_output: ['a b c d', 'd e f g', 'g h i j']

tests.test: print(chunk_words('one two three four five', 2, 0), chunk_words('x  y\n z', 5, 2), chunk_words('', 3, 1))

tests.expected_output:
14 ['a b c', 'b c d', 'c d e']
ValueError

hints: text.split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty pieces.
Keep a start index. Each chunk is words[start:start + size]. Move start forward by size - overlap.
Stop as soon as start + size >= len(words): that chunk already reached the end.
exercises.explanation: Chunk size is the first knob of every RAG system. Small chunks match a question precisely but lose the context around the answer; large ones keep context but dilute the match and fill the prompt. Real systems count tokens rather than words, and prefer to cut at headings, paragraphs or sentences (recursive or structure-aware chunking) so that a table or a function is not split down the middle. Overlap of 10 to 20 percent is a common starting point; the only honest way to choose is to measure retrieval on your own questions.

exercises.title: Dense retrieval: cosine similarity
exercises.statement:
An embedding model turns a query and each chunk into vectors. Retrieval then ranks chunks by how close their vectors are to the query's.

Write cosine(a, b): the dot product divided by the product of the two lengths. If either vector is all zeros, return 0.

Write top_k(query, docs, k): score every vector in docs against query and return the k best as a list of (index, score) pairs, score rounded to 4 places, best first. On a tie the lower index comes first.
hints: Length of a vector: math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v)).
Score every document with its index, then sort by score (highest first) and index (lowest first).
scored = [(i, cosine(query, d)) for i, d in enumerate(docs)], scored.sort(key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])), then round the first k.
exercises.explanation: Cosine similarity ignores length and keeps only direction, which suits embeddings, where direction carries the meaning. Many embedding models return unit-length vectors, and then cosine similarity is just the dot product. Comparing a query with every vector, as here, is exact but takes time proportional to the collection. Vector databases use approximate indexes instead (HNSW graphs, or IVF with product quantisation) that look at a small fraction of the vectors and miss a few true neighbours. Recall of the index, latency and memory are the trade-off you are asked to talk through.

exercises.title: Keyword retrieval: BM25
exercises.statement:
Dense retrieval misses exact strings such as part numbers, names and error codes. BM25 is the keyword ranking that search engines have used for decades, and hybrid search combines the two.

Write bm25(query, docs, k1=1.5, b=0.75). query is a list of words and docs a list of documents, each a list of words. Return one score per document:

  • N is the number of documents, avgdl their average length, n(w) the number of documents that contain word w.
  • idf(w) = ln((N - n(w) + 0.5) / (n(w) + 0.5) + 1).
  • For a document of length dl in which w appears f times, word w contributes idf(w) * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl)).
  • A document's score is the sum over the words of the query (a word repeated in the query counts each time).

tests.test:
docs = [['the', 'cat', 'sat'], ['the', 'dog', 'sat', 'down'], ['a', 'cat', 'and', 'a', 'cat']]
print([round(s, 4) for s in bm25(['cat'], docs)])

docs = [['error', 'xj4410', 'on', 'boot'], ['boot', 'loop', 'after', 'update'], ['update', 'fails', 'with', 'error']]
print([round(s, 4) for s in bm25(['xj4410', 'error'], docs)], [round(s, 4) for s in bm25(['missing'], docs)])

docs = [['a', 'b'], ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g', 'h']]
print([round(s, 4) for s in bm25(['a'], docs)], [round(s, 4) for s in bm25(['a'], docs, b=0)], [round(s, 4) for s in bm25(['b', 'b'], docs)])

hints: Work out N, avgdl and, for each query word, how many documents contain it, before scoring anything.
For each document, doc.count(w) is f and len(doc) is dl. A word that is not in the document adds nothing.
Score: idf * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl)), summed over for w in query (not over a set of the query words).
exercises.solution:
import math


def bm25(query, docs, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
    N = len(docs)
    avgdl = sum(len(d) for d in docs) / N
    scores = []
    for doc in docs:
        s, dl = 0.0, len(doc)
        for w in query:
            n = sum(1 for d in docs if w in d)
            f = doc.count(w)
            if f == 0:
                continue
            idf = math.log((N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5) + 1)
            s += idf * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl))
        scores.append(s)
    return scores
exercises.explanation: BM25 rewards words that are rare in the collection (the idf), rewards repeats with diminishing returns (k1 caps how much a tenth mention adds), and discounts long documents (b). The part number appears in one document, so it carries a high idf and puts that document first, which is exactly what embeddings tend to miss. This idf is the version Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch use; the + 1 keeps it positive even for a word in most documents. In production, BM25 and dense retrieval are run side by side and their rankings fused, the next exercise.

exercises.title: Hybrid search: reciprocal rank fusion
exercises.statement:
BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on different scales, so they cannot simply be added. Reciprocal rank fusion combines rankings using only the positions.

Write rrf(rankings, k=60). rankings is a list of rankings; each ranking is a list of document ids, best first. A document at position r in a ranking (r starts at 1) gets 1 / (k + r) from that ranking; a ranking that does not contain it gives nothing. Return a list of (doc_id, score) pairs, score rounded to 6 places, best first; on a tie the smaller id comes first.
hints: Use a dictionary from document id to its running score.
for ranking in rankings: for r, doc in enumerate(ranking, start=1): score[doc] = score.get(doc, 0) + 1 / (k + r).
Sort score.items() with key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]), then round each score.
exercises.explanation: A document ranked well by both retrievers rises to the top, even if neither ranked it first: p2 wins because it is second in one list and first in the other. k = 60 comes from the original paper (Cormack et al., 2009) and is the default in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and most vector databases; a larger k flattens the difference between first and tenth place. RRF needs no tuning and no score normalisation, which is why it is the standard first answer to 'how do you combine keyword and vector search'. A cross-encoder reranker over the fused top 50 is the usual second step.

exercises.title: Diverse results: maximal marginal relevance
exercises.statement:
The top five chunks are often five copies of the same paragraph. Maximal marginal relevance picks results that are relevant and different from the ones already picked.

Write mmr(query_sims, doc_sims, k, lam). query_sims[i] is the similarity of document i to the query and doc_sims[i][j] the similarity between documents i and j.

Pick k documents one at a time. The first is the one most similar to the query. After that, each candidate d not yet picked scores lam * query_sims[d] - (1 - lam) * (its largest similarity to any picked document), and the highest score is picked next. On a tie the lower index wins. Return the picked indices in the order they were picked.
exercises.starter:
def mmr(query_sims, doc_sims, k, lam):
    pass
hints: Keep a list of picked indices. The first pick is the index of the largest query similarity.
For each remaining candidate, its redundancy is max(doc_sims[d][s] for s in picked). Its score combines relevance and redundancy with lam.
Loop while len(picked) < min(k, n): choose max(candidates, key=lambda d: (score(d), -d)) and append it.
exercises.explanation: With lam = 1 MMR is plain ranking by relevance and returns the near-duplicate documents 0 and 1 together. At 0.5 the second pick is document 2, less relevant but saying something new. At lam = 0 only novelty counts. Values around 0.5 to 0.7 are typical; LangChain and most vector stores offer MMR as a search option. It matters most when the context window is small and every chunk in it has to earn its place.

exercises.title: Packing a context: budget and order
exercises.statement:
Retrieved chunks must fit the model's token budget, and models use the beginning and the end of a long context better than the middle (the 'lost in the middle' effect).

Write pack_context(chunks, budget). Each chunk is a tuple (score, tokens, text).

  1. Choose: go through the chunks from the highest score down (on a tie, the one that came first in the input). Take a chunk if it still fits in what is left of budget; otherwise skip it and carry on with the next.
  2. Order: place the chosen chunks so that the best is first, the second best is last, the third is second, the fourth is second to last, and so on, working inward from both ends.

Return the texts in their final order.
hints: Sort the indices by score, highest first, keeping input order on ties: sorted(range(len(chunks)), key=lambda i: (-chunks[i][0], i)).
Choosing is greedy: keep a running total of tokens and skip any chunk that would go over the budget.
Ordering: build front and back lists. Chosen chunk 0 goes on front, 1 on back, 2 on front, and so on. The answer is front + back[::-1].
exercises.explanation: Greedy filling by score is what most RAG frameworks do, and skipping a chunk that does not fit, rather than stopping, keeps small useful chunks in. The order follows Liu et al. (2023), who found accuracy highest when the answer sits at the start or the end of the context and lowest in the middle; LangChain's LongContextReorder does this same placement. Long-context models have reduced the effect but not removed it. The better fix is to retrieve less and rerank well, so that what goes into the prompt is short and good.

exercises.title: Recall@k and mean reciprocal rank
exercises.statement:
Before judging the answers of a RAG system, measure its retriever. You need a set of questions, each with the ids of the chunks that answer it.

  • recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k): the fraction of the relevant ids that appear among the first k retrieved. If relevant is empty, return 0.
  • mrr(runs): runs is a list of (retrieved, relevant) pairs, one per question. For each, the reciprocal rank is 1 / r where r is the position (from 1) of the first relevant id in retrieved, or 0 if none appears. Return the mean.
hints: Recall counts how many relevant ids are in retrieved[:k], divided by how many relevant ids there are.
For MRR, walk each retrieved list with enumerate(retrieved, start=1) and stop at the first relevant id.
mrr: total the reciprocal ranks (0 when nothing relevant is found) and divide by len(runs).
exercises.explanation: Recall@k asks whether the answer made it into the prompt at all, which bounds everything the generator can do: if retrieval misses, no prompt fixes it. MRR asks how high the first good chunk was, which matters because models attend more to the beginning and end of the context. Fifty to a hundred questions written by hand, with the chunk ids that answer them, is the most valuable asset of a RAG project. Interviewers ask how you built yours.

exercises.title: Exact match and token F1
exercises.statement:
For questions with short answers, generated answers are scored against reference answers the way the SQuAD benchmark does it.

Write normalize(s): lowercase; remove punctuation (every character in string.punctuation); remove the words a, an and the; join the remaining words with single spaces.

Write exact_match(pred, golds) and f1(pred, golds). golds is a list of acceptable answers; each function returns the best score over them.

  • Exact match is 1 if the normalised strings are equal, else 0.
  • F1 compares the words of the normalised strings: the overlap counts each word as many times as it appears in both (a Counter intersection). precision = overlap / words in pred, recall = overlap / words in gold, F1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall), and 0 if the overlap is 0.

tests.test: print(repr(normalize('The  Eiffel Tower!')), exact_match('the eiffel tower', ['Eiffel Tower']), exact_match('Paris, France', ['Paris']))
print(round(f1('Paris, France', ['Paris']), 4), round(f1('in the year 1889', ['1889', 'year 1889']), 4), f1('London', ['Paris']))
print(round(f1('a cat a cat', ['cat']), 4), round(f1('cat cat dog', ['cat cat cat']), 4), f1('the', ['a']))

hints: Remove punctuation with s.translate(str.maketrans('', '', string.punctuation)), then split into words and drop the articles.
For F1, count the words of each side with Counter and take sum((Counter(p) & Counter(g)).values()) as the overlap.
When both normalised strings are empty (an answer of only articles), treat F1 as 1 if they are equal; when only one is empty, the overlap is 0. Take max over the golds.
exercises.explanation: Exact match is harsh: 'Paris, France' scores 0 against 'Paris'. Token F1 gives partial credit, 0.67 here. Both are cheap, repeatable and blind to meaning, so 'the capital of France' against 'Paris' scores 0. That gap is why RAG evaluation also uses an LLM as a judge with a written rubric, checks that each claim is supported by a retrieved chunk (faithfulness), and keeps a small human-reviewed set to check the judge itself. Being able to say which metric you used, and what it misses, is most of the evaluation question in an interview.

exercises.title: Graded relevance: nDCG@k
exercises.statement:
Recall treats every relevant chunk alike. When chunks are graded (0 for useless, 1 for related, 3 for the exact answer), nDCG rewards putting the best ones first.

Write ndcg_at_k(retrieved, gains, k). gains maps a document id to its grade; ids not in it have grade 0.

  • DCG = sum over positions i = 1..k of (2 ** grade - 1) / log2(i + 1), for the first k retrieved ids.
  • IDCG is the DCG of the best possible ranking: all graded ids sorted from the highest grade down, cut to k.
  • Return DCG / IDCG, or 0 if IDCG is 0.
hints: Write a small helper dcg(grades) that takes the grades in ranked order.
The grades of the retrieved list are [gains.get(d, 0) for d in retrieved[:k]]. The ideal list is sorted(gains.values(), reverse=True)[:k].
dcg = sum((2 ** g - 1) / math.log2(i + 1) for i, g in enumerate(grades, start=1)).
exercises.explanation: The logarithm makes position 1 count fully, position 2 count 63%, position 10 count 29%. Dividing by the ideal puts every query on a 0 to 1 scale, so queries with many or few relevant chunks can be averaged. 2 ** grade - 1 makes a grade-3 chunk worth seven grade-1 chunks, which says that the exact answer matters much more than something related. nDCG is the standard metric of search and recommendation teams; for RAG, recall@k for the retriever and nDCG for the reranker is a sound pair.

exercises.title: The fine-tuning loss, with the prompt masked
exercises.statement:
In supervised fine-tuning (SFT) the model learns to produce the response, not to repeat the prompt, so the loss is taken over the response tokens only.

Write sft_loss(logprobs, mask): logprobs[i] is the model's log-probability of the correct token at position i, and mask[i] is 1 for response tokens and 0 for prompt tokens. Return the mean of -logprobs[i] over the positions where mask[i] is 1 (0 if there are none).

Write perplexity(logprobs): exp of the mean of -logprobs over all positions.
hints: Select the positions with mask[i] == 1 using zip(logprobs, mask).
The loss is the average negative log-probability over those positions. Perplexity uses every position.
picked = [-lp for lp, m in zip(logprobs, mask) if m], return sum(picked) / len(picked) if picked else 0. perplexity: math.exp(-sum(logprobs) / len(logprobs)).
exercises.explanation: Masking the prompt is what TRL's completion-only training and Hugging Face's -100 labels do. Without it the model also spends its capacity learning to predict the questions in your data set. Perplexity is the exponent of the average loss: a perplexity of 4 means the model is as unsure as a fair choice among four tokens. It is how pretraining runs are compared, and it says little about whether answers are helpful, which is why chat models are judged by evaluations of their answers rather than by perplexity.

exercises.title: LoRA: a low-rank update
exercises.statement:
LoRA freezes a weight matrix W (d_out by d_in) and learns two small ones: A (r by d_in) and B (d_out by r). The layer computes W x + (alpha / r) * B (A x).

Matrices are lists of rows; vectors are lists.

  • matvec(M, x): the product of a matrix and a vector.
  • lora_forward(W, A, B, x, alpha, r): the output of the adapted layer.
  • merge(W, A, B, alpha, r): the single matrix W + (alpha / r) * B A, so that serving needs no extra work.
  • lora_params(d_in, d_out, r): the number of trainable numbers, r * d_in + d_out * r.
hints: matvec: one dot product per row: [sum(m * v for m, v in zip(row, x)) for row in M].
The forward pass is matvec(W, x) plus alpha / r times matvec(B, matvec(A, x)).
For merge, entry (i, j) of B A is sum(B[i][t] * A[t][j] for t in range(r)). Add alpha / r times it to W[i][j].
exercises.explanation: For a 4,096 by 4,096 projection, rank 8 trains 65,536 numbers instead of 16.8 million: 0.39%. Optimiser state shrinks by the same factor, which is what lets a 7B model be tuned on one GPU, and with the frozen weights in 4 bits (QLoRA) on a small one. B starts at zero, so the adapted model starts out exactly equal to the original (the last test). Merging after training gives back one matrix of the original shape, so serving costs nothing extra; keeping adapters separate instead lets one server switch between many fine-tunes. Which matrices to adapt (attention projections only, or the MLP too) and the rank are the two choices you are asked to justify.

exercises.title: Reward models: the Bradley-Terry loss
exercises.statement:
RLHF first trains a reward model that gives an answer a score. It is trained on pairs: the preferred answer should score higher.

  • win_prob(r_a, r_b): the probability that answer A is preferred, sigmoid(r_a - r_b) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(r_a - r_b))).
  • rm_loss(pairs): pairs is a list of (r_chosen, r_rejected). Return the mean of -log(win_prob(r_chosen, r_rejected)).
  • accuracy(pairs): the fraction of pairs in which the chosen answer has the strictly higher reward.
hints: Only the difference of the two rewards matters. Adding the same number to both changes nothing.
rm_loss is the average of -math.log(win_prob(c, r)) over the pairs.
accuracy: sum(1 for c, r in pairs if c > r) / len(pairs).
exercises.explanation: This is the Bradley-Terry model of comparisons, the same one behind chess ratings and the LMArena leaderboard. A reward model's accuracy on held-out pairs is often only about 65 to 75%, partly because the people labelling the pairs disagree with each other. The second stage of RLHF optimises the language model against this score with PPO, plus a penalty for moving far from the original model; without the penalty the model learns to exploit the reward model's mistakes, which is called reward hacking. DPO, the exercise before, folds the two stages into one loss.

exercises.title: Direct preference optimisation
exercises.statement:
Preference data says, for one prompt, which of two answers people preferred. DPO trains on it directly, with no separate reward model and no reinforcement learning loop.

Inputs are summed log-probabilities of whole answers: pi_c and pi_r from the model being trained for the chosen and rejected answer, and ref_c and ref_r from a frozen copy of it (the reference).

  • margin(pi_c, pi_r, ref_c, ref_r, beta) returns beta * ((pi_c - ref_c) - (pi_r - ref_r)).
  • dpo_loss(pi_c, pi_r, ref_c, ref_r, beta) returns -log(sigmoid(margin)), computed without overflow for large margins of either sign: -log(sigmoid(z)) equals log(1 + exp(-z)), and for negative z it equals -z + log(1 + exp(z)).
hints: The margin compares how much the model has moved toward the chosen answer with how much it has moved toward the rejected one, each measured against the reference.
With z = margin(...), the loss is -log(1 / (1 + exp(-z))), which simplifies to log(1 + exp(-z)). math.log1p(x) computes log(1 + x) accurately.
if z >= 0: return math.log1p(math.exp(-z)) and otherwise return -z + math.log1p(math.exp(z)). Both branches only ever take exp of a number that is not positive.
exercises.explanation: At the start the model equals the reference, the margin is 0 and the loss is ln 2 = 0.6931. Raising the chosen answer and lowering the rejected one, relative to the reference, makes the margin positive and the loss small. beta sets how far the model may drift from the reference; it plays the part of the KL penalty in RLHF. Rafailov et al. (2023) showed that this loss optimises the same objective as RLHF with PPO, which is why most open models moved to DPO or its variants. In an interview, contrast it with RLHF: no reward model to train, no sampling during training, far more stable; and with GRPO, the reinforcement learning method DeepSeek used to train reasoning from rewards that can be checked automatically.

exercises.title: Checking a tool call before running it
exercises.statement:
A model asks for a tool by writing JSON such as {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune"}}. Never run it unchecked: the model can invent tools and arguments.

Write check_call(text, tools). tools maps a tool name to {"params": {argument: type}, "required": [arguments]}, where a type is one of "string", "integer", "number" and "boolean". Return "ok" or the first problem found, checking in this order:

  1. "error: not valid JSON" if text does not parse, or does not parse to an object with a string name and an object arguments.
  2. "error: unknown tool NAME".
  3. "error: unexpected argument X" for an argument the tool does not have (the first such in alphabetical order).
  4. "error: missing argument X" for a required argument that is absent (in the order of required).
  5. "error: argument X must be TYPE" for a value of the wrong type (in the order of params). A bool is not an integer or a number here, and an integer counts as a number.

tests.test:
print(check_call('{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune", "days": 3}}', TOOLS))
print(check_call('{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune"', TOOLS))
print(check_call('{"name": "book_flight", "arguments": {}}', TOOLS))
tests.expected_output:
ok
error: not valid JSON
error: unknown tool book_flight

tests.test:
print(check_call('{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"days": 2}}', TOOLS))
print(check_call('{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Pune", "units": "C", "lang": "en"}}', TOOLS))
print(check_call('{"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": 42}}', TOOLS))
tests.expected_output:
error: missing argument city
error: unexpected argument lang
error: argument city must be string

tests.test:
print(check_call('{"name": "convert", "arguments": {"amount": 10, "exact": true}}', TOOLS))
print(check_call('{"name": "convert", "arguments": {"amount": true}}', TOOLS))
print(check_call('[1, 2]', TOOLS), check_call('{"name": "convert", "arguments": {"amount": 2.5, "exact": 1}}', TOOLS))
tests.expected_output:
ok
error: argument amount must be number
error: not valid JSON error: argument exact must be boolean

hints: Parse with json.loads inside try/except ValueError, then check that the result is a dict with the right kinds of name and arguments.
Each type name maps to a test: "string" is isinstance(v, str); "integer" is an int that is not a bool; "number" is an int or float that is not a bool.
Follow the order exactly: unknown tool, then sorted(set(args) - set(params)), then required, then params in order.
exercises.explanation: The error messages are written for the model, not for a person: an agent loop sends them back as the tool's result, and a good message lets the model correct itself on the next step. This is the job of JSON Schema in function calling and in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where every tool a server offers is described by a name, a description and an input schema. Providers' structured-output modes constrain decoding so that the JSON always parses, but they do not check that a tool exists for your application or that a value makes sense: that check stays in your code.
exercises.unit: Agents and LLM apps in production

exercises.title: What a request costs
exercises.statement:
LLM APIs charge per million tokens, with different prices for input, for input read from the provider's prompt cache, and for output.

Write request_cost(prompt_tokens, cached_tokens, output_tokens, prices). prices is a dictionary with "input", "cached" and "output", each in dollars per million tokens. cached_tokens is the part of prompt_tokens that was read from the cache; the rest is charged at the input price. Return the cost in dollars.

Write monthly_cost(requests_per_day, prompt_tokens, cached_tokens, output_tokens, prices, days=30).

tests.test:
Q = {'input': 0.15, 'cached': 0.075, 'output': 0.6}
print(round(request_cost(0, 0, 0, Q), 6), round(request_cost(1000000, 1000000, 1000000, Q), 6), round(monthly_cost(1000, 2000, 0, 300, Q, days=7), 4))

hints: Split the prompt into the cached part and the rest, then price the three parts.
Prices are per million tokens: divide each token count by 1,000,000 before multiplying.
((prompt_tokens - cached_tokens) * prices['input'] + cached_tokens * prices['cached'] + output_tokens * prices['output']) / 1e6. The monthly cost multiplies by requests per day and days.
exercises.explanation: With these prices a 10,000-token prompt costs four times its 500-token answer, and reading 8,000 of those tokens from the cache cuts the bill from $0.0375 to $0.0159 a request: at 20,000 requests a day, $22,500 a month becomes $9,540. The prices are examples of the shape of real price lists, not any provider's current prices. The levers are always the same: shorter prompts, cached prefixes, a smaller model for easy requests (routing), batching jobs that can wait, and capping output length. 'How would you cut the bill without losing quality?' is a standard design question, and the answer starts with this arithmetic and a dashboard of tokens per feature.
exercises.unit: Agents and LLM apps in production

exercises.title: An agent loop with a step limit
exercises.statement:
An agent is a loop: the model looks at the conversation so far and either calls a tool or gives a final answer; the tool's result is added to the conversation; repeat.

Write run_agent(model, tools, task, max_steps).

  • The history starts as [('user', task)]. Each step, call model(history). It returns either {'answer': text} or {'tool': name, 'args': {...}}.
  • An answer ends the run: return (text, steps) where steps is the number of model calls made.
  • A tool call appends ('call', name, args) to the history, runs tools[name](**args) and appends ('result', name, value). If the tool does not exist, the result is 'error: unknown tool'; if it raises an exception e, the result is 'error: ' + str(e). The loop goes on either way.
  • After max_steps model calls without an answer, return ('stopped: step limit', max_steps).
exercises.starter:
def run_agent(model, tools, task, max_steps):
    pass

tests.expected_output:
('got 0.25 after 2 tool calls', 3)
('stopped: step limit', 3) 3 ('result', 'nope', 'error: unknown tool')

hints: Keep history as a list of tuples and a counter of model calls. The loop runs at most max_steps times.
Look the tool up with tools.get(name). Wrap the call in try/except Exception as e.
Each step: steps += 1, out = model(history); if 'answer' in out: return (out['answer'], steps); otherwise append the call and the result. After the loop, return the step-limit message.
exercises.explanation: This is the ReAct pattern without the framework: reason, act, observe, repeat. Every agent library, from LangGraph to the OpenAI Agents SDK, has this loop at its centre, and interviewers increasingly ask you to write it. Two choices here carry over to production. Errors go back to the model as results instead of crashing the run, so it can try something else; and a hard step limit stops a confused model from looping and spending money. Real agents add a token or cost budget, a timeout per tool, logging of every step (a trace), and an evaluation that checks the end state of the task rather than the wording of the answer.
exercises.unit: Agents and LLM apps in production

exercises.title: A token-bucket rate limiter
exercises.statement:
LLM providers limit requests and tokens per minute, and so must your own API. The token bucket allows short bursts while holding the average rate.

Write class TokenBucket with __init__(self, rate, capacity) and allow(self, now, cost=1).

  • The bucket starts full, with capacity tokens, at the time of the first call.
  • Tokens refill at rate per second, continuously, up to capacity.
  • allow(now, cost) first adds the tokens earned since the previous call (now is in seconds and never goes backwards), then, if at least cost tokens are there, removes them and returns True; otherwise returns False and removes nothing.

tests.test:
b = TokenBucket(1, 3)
print([b.allow(0) for _ in range(4)], b.allow(0.5), b.allow(1.0), b.allow(1.1))
tests.expected_output: [True, True, True, False] False True False

tests.test:
b = TokenBucket(2, 4)
print(b.allow(0, 4), b.allow(1, 3), b.allow(1.5, 3), b.allow(100, 4), b.allow(100, 5))

hints: Store tokens, capacity, rate and the time of the last call (None before the first call).
On each call: if there was a previous call, add (now - last) * rate and cap at capacity; then remember now as the last time.

exercises.title: A response cache for an LLM app
exercises.statement:
Many users ask the same thing. A cache that returns a stored answer saves money and seconds, but only answers produced with temperature 0 are worth reusing.

Write class PromptCache with __init__(self, capacity), get(self, prompt, model, temperature) and put(self, prompt, model, temperature, answer).

  • The key is (model, prompt) with the prompt lowercased and its whitespace collapsed to single spaces (strip the ends).
  • If temperature is not 0, put stores nothing and get returns None without counting anything.
  • Otherwise get returns the stored answer or None, and counts a hit or a miss in self.hits and self.misses.
  • At most capacity answers are kept. When a new one would exceed it, the least recently used is removed; both get (on a hit) and put count as a use.

c.put('a', 'm', 0, 1)
c.put('b', 'm', 0, 2)
c.get('a', 'm', 0)
c.put('c', 'm', 0, 3)
print(c.get('a', 'm', 0), c.get('b', 'm', 0), c.get('c', 'm', 0), c.hits, c.misses)

c = PromptCache(5)
c.put('x', 'm', 0.7, 'creative')
print(c.get('x', 'm', 0), c.get('x', 'm', 0.7), c.hits, c.misses)
c.put('x', 'm', 0, 'one')
c.put('X', 'm', 0, 'two')

hints: An OrderedDict remembers order: move_to_end(key) marks a key as just used and popitem(last=False) removes the oldest.
Write a helper for the key: (model, ' '.join(prompt.lower().split())).
In put: store the answer, move_to_end, and if len(self.store) > self.capacity, popitem(last=False). Name the dictionary self.store.
exercises.explanation: An exact cache like this one catches repeated questions, retries and repeated test runs. A semantic cache goes further and returns a stored answer when a new question's embedding is close enough to an old one, which saves more and risks answering a different question. Do not confuse either with prompt caching by the provider, which reuses the processed prefix of a prompt (the system prompt, the tool definitions, long documents) and charges less for those input tokens. To benefit from that, put what stays the same at the start of the prompt and what changes at the end.

exercises.title: Reading a streamed answer
exercises.statement:
Chat APIs stream answers as server-sent events: lines of the form data: {...}, separated by blank lines, ending with data: [DONE]. The network delivers them in arbitrary pieces, so a line can be split across two chunks.

Write read_stream(chunks). chunks is a list of strings as they arrived. Join the text into lines (split on \n); for each complete line:

  • ignore empty lines and lines starting with : (comments, used as keep-alives);
  • a line data: [DONE] ends the stream; ignore anything after it;
  • any other data: line holds JSON with a "delta" string: append it to the answer.

Return the full answer. Only complete lines count: a final piece with no \n after it is not processed.
hints: Keep a buffer of text not yet processed. Add each chunk to it, then cut off every complete line.
while '\n' in buffer: line, buffer = buffer.split('\n', 1). Whatever stays in the buffer waits for the next chunk.
For a data line, payload = line[len('data: '):]; stop if it is [DONE], else answer.append(json.loads(payload)['delta']).
exercises.explanation: Streaming is why chat feels fast: the first words appear after the time-to-first-token, long before the whole answer is ready. The trap is assuming one chunk is one event; the second test splits JSON in the middle of a key, as real networks do. Providers differ in what the JSON holds (OpenAI-style choices[0].delta.content, Anthropic's typed events such as content_block_delta), but the framing is the same. A 'streaming parser' is one of the practical coding tasks in AI engineering interviews, sometimes with tool-call arguments that arrive as JSON in pieces.

FROM transactions
WHERE kind = 'debit'

exercises.statement:
The bank's tables are under Already defined for you:

  • customers(id, name, city, joined): city can be NULL; joined is a date such as '2026-01-05'.
  • accounts(id, customer_id, type, opened): a customer can have several accounts, or none.
  • transactions(id, account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant, category): ts is a date, amount is positive, kind is 'credit' (money in) or 'debit' (money out).

Write QUERY: each customer's two largest debits, with columns name, amount, merchant and rnk (1 for their largest). Break ties between equal amounts by the lower transaction id. Order by name, then rnk.
hints: Join transactions to accounts to customers, keep debits, and number each customer's rows from the largest down.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.id ORDER BY t.amount DESC, t.id) restarts at 1 for every customer. A window function cannot go in WHERE, so compute it in a subquery or a WITH clause first.
WITH ranked AS (SELECT c.name, t.amount, t.merchant, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rnk FROM ...) SELECT name, amount, merchant, rnk FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 2 ORDER BY name, rnk.
exercises.solution:
QUERY = """
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT c.name, t.amount, t.merchant,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.id ORDER BY t.amount DESC, t.id) AS rnk
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id
    WHERE t.kind = 'debit'
)
SELECT name, amount, merchant, rnk
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY name, rnk
"""
exercises.explanation: 'Top n per group' is the most asked window-function question. ROW_NUMBER gives every row a different number, so ties are broken by the ORDER BY; RANK would give two equal amounts the same rank and possibly return three rows; DENSE_RANK is what you want for 'the second-highest distinct value'. Kiran's two largest come from two different accounts, which is why the partition is by customer and not by account. Ravi paid rent of 18,000 twice: ROW_NUMBER still gives the two payments ranks 1 and 2, in the order of their ids.

hints: The sign comes from a CASE on kind.
SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ts, id) adds up every row up to and including the current one, in that order.

SELECT id, ts, CASE WHEN kind = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS change, SUM(CASE WHEN kind = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (ORDER BY ts, id) AS balance FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 101 ORDER BY ts, id.

QUERY = """
SELECT id, ts,
       CASE WHEN kind = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS change,
       SUM(CASE WHEN kind = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (ORDER BY ts, id) AS balance
FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 101
ORDER BY ts, id
"""
exercises.explanation: With ORDER BY inside OVER, SUM becomes a running total. Including id in the window's order matters on days with two transactions: with only ts, rows on the same date are peers and all get the day's closing balance, a subtle default (the RANGE frame) that interviewers like to ask about. For every account at once, add PARTITION BY account_id.

exercises.title: Month-over-month change
exercises.statement:
The bank's tables are under Already defined for you:

  • customers(id, name, city, joined): city can be NULL; joined is a date such as '2026-01-05'.
  • accounts(id, customer_id, type, opened): a customer can have several accounts, or none.
  • transactions(id, account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant, category): ts is a date, amount is positive, kind is 'credit' (money in) or 'debit' (money out).

Write QUERY: for each customer and each month in which they made debits, columns name, month (such as '2026-03'), spent (total debits that month) and prev (their total in the previous month in which they made debits, NULL for their first such month). Order by name, then month.
hints: First build one row per customer and month: join to customers, keep debits, strftime('%Y-%m', t.ts) is the month, and group.
Then LAG(spent) OVER (PARTITION BY name ORDER BY month) looks one row back within the same customer.

WITH monthly AS (SELECT c.id, c.name, strftime('%Y-%m', t.ts) AS month, SUM(t.amount) AS spent FROM ... GROUP BY c.id, month) SELECT name, month, spent, LAG(spent) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly ORDER BY name, month.
exercises.solution:
QUERY = """
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT c.id, c.name, strftime('%Y-%m', t.ts) AS month, SUM(t.amount) AS spent
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id
    WHERE t.kind = 'debit'
    GROUP BY c.id, c.name, month
)
SELECT name, month, spent,
       LAG(spent) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month) AS prev
FROM monthly
ORDER BY name, month
"""
exercises.explanation: Aggregate first, then apply the window: window functions run after GROUP BY, which is why the monthly totals go in a WITH clause. LAG looks at the previous row, not the previous calendar month: in the last test the row before March is January, because Ravi spent nothing in February. If the question means the calendar month, join each month to the month before instead, or fill the gaps first. Growth is then spent / prev - 1, and 'month-over-month growth per customer' is a standard analytics question at banks and in e-commerce.

exercises.title: Duplicates to remove
exercises.statement:
The bank's tables are under Already defined for you:

  • customers(id, name, city, joined): city can be NULL; joined is a date such as '2026-01-05'.
  • accounts(id, customer_id, type, opened): a customer can have several accounts, or none.
  • transactions(id, account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant, category): ts is a date, amount is positive, kind is 'credit' (money in) or 'debit' (money out).

Card networks sometimes send a charge twice. Treat two transactions as duplicates when they have the same account_id, ts, amount, kind and merchant. Write QUERY: the id of every transaction that should be deleted, keeping the one with the lowest id in each group of duplicates. Order by id.
hints: Number the rows within each group of identical transactions, lowest id first. Every row numbered 2 or more is a duplicate.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant ORDER BY id).
WITH numbered AS (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rn FROM transactions) SELECT id FROM numbered WHERE rn > 1 ORDER BY id. GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 with MIN(id) works too.
exercises.solution:
QUERY = """
WITH numbered AS (
    SELECT id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant ORDER BY id) AS rn
    FROM transactions
)
SELECT id
FROM numbered
WHERE rn > 1
ORDER BY id
"""
exercises.explanation: The same pattern removes duplicates in any pipeline: partition by what defines 'the same', order by what decides which copy to keep, keep row 1. As a delete: DELETE FROM transactions WHERE id IN (this query). The edge cases are the definition: the Ola ride is a different merchant and stays, and a credit is not a duplicate of a debit. In an interview, ask what makes two rows the same before writing anything.

exercises.title: Unusually large debits
exercises.statement:
The bank's tables are under Already defined for you:

  • customers(id, name, city, joined): city can be NULL; joined is a date such as '2026-01-05'.
  • accounts(id, customer_id, type, opened): a customer can have several accounts, or none.
  • transactions(id, account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant, category): ts is a date, amount is positive, kind is 'credit' (money in) or 'debit' (money out).

A simple fraud rule flags a debit that is more than three times the customer's average debit. Write QUERY with columns name, id, amount and avg_debit (the customer's average over all their debits, rounded to 2 places). Order by id.
hints: Every debit needs its customer's average next to it: an aggregate without collapsing the rows. That is a window function with PARTITION BY and no ORDER BY.
AVG(t.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY c.id) over the joined debits. Filter in an outer query.

WITH d AS (SELECT c.name, t.id, t.amount, AVG(t.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY c.id) AS av FROM ... WHERE t.kind = 'debit') SELECT name, id, amount, ROUND(av, 2) AS avg_debit FROM d WHERE amount > 3 * av ORDER BY id.
exercises.solution:
QUERY = """
WITH d AS (
    SELECT c.name, t.id, t.amount, AVG(t.amount) OVER (PARTITION BY c.id) AS av
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = a.customer_id
    WHERE t.kind = 'debit'
)
SELECT name, id, amount, ROUND(av, 2) AS avg_debit
FROM d
WHERE amount > 3 * av
ORDER BY id
"""
exercises.explanation: A window aggregate keeps every row and adds the group's value beside it, which a GROUP BY cannot. Compare with the unrounded average and round only for display. As a fraud rule this is crude: the large purchase inflates the very average it is compared with, and a customer with one debit can never be flagged. Real systems compare with the customer's history before the transaction (a window that ends one row back), use medians, and feed such features to a model, as in the card-fraud replay.

exercises.statement:
The bank's tables are under Already defined for you:

  • customers(id, name, city, joined): city can be NULL; joined is a date such as '2026-01-05'.
  • accounts(id, customer_id, type, opened): a customer can have several accounts, or none.
  • transactions(id, account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant, category): ts is a date, amount is positive, kind is 'credit' (money in) or 'debit' (money out).

Write QUERY: the name of every customer who made transactions (of any kind) on at least 3 consecutive calendar days, across all their accounts. Order by name.
hints: First reduce the data to one row per customer and day with SELECT DISTINCT, since several transactions on one day count once.
The gaps and islands trick: number each customer's days in order with ROW_NUMBER(). Within a run of consecutive days, julianday(day) - row_number is the same value; it jumps when a day is skipped.
Group by customer and that difference, keep groups with COUNT(*) >= 3, and select the distinct names.
exercises.solution:
QUERY = """
WITH days AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id, t.ts AS day
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON a.id = t.account_id
),
islands AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           julianday(day) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY day) AS grp
    FROM days
)
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM islands i
JOIN customers c ON c.id = i.customer_id
GROUP BY i.customer_id, i.grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY c.name
"""
exercises.explanation: Consecutive days minus their position in the list stay constant: 7, 8, 9, 10 minus 1, 2, 3, 4 is 6 every time. Each constant is an island. julianday makes the dates numbers, so the run across the end of February in the last test works without any calendar arithmetic. The same trick finds login streaks, consecutive months of missed payments, and sessions; it is the hardest common SQL pattern, and the one that separates candidates.

exercises.statement:
The bank's tables are under Already defined for you:

  • customers(id, name, city, joined): city can be NULL; joined is a date such as '2026-01-05'.
  • accounts(id, customer_id, type, opened): a customer can have several accounts, or none.
  • transactions(id, account_id, ts, amount, kind, merchant, category): ts is a date, amount is positive, kind is 'credit' (money in) or 'debit' (money out).

Write QUERY: for each month in which customers joined (a cohort, such as '2026-01'), columns cohort, customers (how many joined that month) and retained (how many of them made at least one transaction, of any kind, in the next calendar month). Order by cohort.
hints: The cohort is strftime('%Y-%m', joined). The next month is strftime('%Y-%m', date(joined, 'start of month', '+1 month')); going through the first of the month avoids surprises on the 31st.
For each customer, decide whether they were active in that next month with EXISTS over their accounts and transactions. That gives 1 or 0 per customer.
Group by cohort: COUNT(*) AS customers, SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (...) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained.
exercises.solution:
QUERY = """
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', c.joined) AS cohort,
       COUNT(*) AS customers,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
               FROM accounts a
               JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.id
               WHERE a.customer_id = c.id
                 AND strftime('%Y-%m', t.ts) = strftime('%Y-%m', date(c.joined, 'start of month', '+1 month'))
           ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retained
FROM customers c
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort
"""
exercises.explanation: Cohort retention is the standard way to ask whether a product keeps its users: group people by when they started, and measure each group later. The rate is retained / customers, and a full retention table has a column for each month after joining. Two details carry the marks: a customer with no transactions must still be counted in customers (no inner join that drops them), and 'next month' must cross the end of the year, as in the last test. date(joined, '+1 month') alone turns 31 January into 3 March in SQLite, which is why the hint goes through the start of the month.

exercises.title: A fraud alert and Bayes' rule
exercises.statement:
A fraud model flags transactions. Write p_fraud_given_alert(base_rate, recall, false_alarm_rate):

  • base_rate is the share of transactions that are fraud, P(F);
  • recall is the share of fraud the model flags, P(alert | F);
  • false_alarm_rate is the share of honest transactions it flags, P(alert | not F).

Return P(F | alert), the probability that a flagged transaction is really fraud. Also write alerts_per_fraud(base_rate, recall, false_alarm_rate): how many alerts the team reviews for each real fraud caught, which is 1 / P(F | alert).
hints: Bayes' rule: P(F | alert) = P(alert | F) P(F) / P(alert).
P(alert) has two parts: frauds that are flagged and honest transactions that are flagged.
p_alert = recall * base_rate + false_alarm_rate * (1 - base_rate), then recall * base_rate / p_alert.
exercises.explanation: A model that catches 95% of fraud with a 2% false-alarm rate sounds excellent, yet only 8.7% of its alerts are fraud: an analyst reviews 11.5 alerts per real case, because honest transactions outnumber fraud 500 to 1. This base-rate effect is the most common probability question in data interviews (asked as a disease test, a spam filter or a fraud alert), and it is why precision, not accuracy, is the number a fraud team lives by. The third test shows the lever: cutting false alarms tenfold matters far more than raising recall.

exercises.statement:
A loan pays a profit of 1,200 if repaid and loses 9,000 if it defaults. Write two functions over a discrete distribution given as parallel lists values and probs (the probabilities add up to 1):

  • expected(values, probs): the sum of value times probability.
  • variance(values, probs): the expected squared distance from the expected value.

Also write break_even_default(gain, loss): the default probability at which the expected profit of the loan is exactly 0.
hints: expected is one sum over zip(values, probs).
Variance: first the mean m, then sum(p * (v - m) ** 2 ...).
Break-even: solve (1 - d) * gain - d * loss = 0 for d: d = gain / (gain + loss).
exercises.explanation: At a 10% default rate the loan expects to earn 180, with a standard deviation of about 3,060: profitable on average and very risky one at a time, which is why lenders hold many loans. The break-even default rate, 11.8% here, is how a credit model's probability turns into a lending decision; a bank then adds a margin for capital and costs. Expected value with a cost on each kind of mistake is also how to choose a model's threshold, a later exercise.

m, lo, hi = mean_ci(xs)
print(round(hi - lo, 4), lo < 100 < hi)

The standard error is s / math.sqrt(n).

exercises.solution:
import math


def mean_ci(xs, z=1.96):
    n = len(xs)
    m = sum(xs) / n
    s = math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (n - 1))
    half = z * s / math.sqrt(n)
    return (round(m, 4), round(m - half, 4), round(m + half, 4))
exercises.explanation: The interval narrows with the square root of n: four times the data for half the width. With 400 draws of spread 15, the width is about 3. Say it correctly in an interview: the procedure captures the true mean in 95% of repeated samples; it is not a 95% probability that this particular interval holds it. Dividing by n - 1 corrects for measuring spread around the sample's own mean, which is a little too close to the data.

exercises.statement:

  • p_two_sided(z): the probability that a standard normal is at least |z| away from 0 in either direction.
  • z_test(sample_mean, mu0, sd, n): the z-statistic (sample_mean - mu0) / (sd / sqrt(n)) and its two-sided p-value, as a pair (z, p), both rounded to 4 places.
hints: Two-sided means both tails: the probability beyond +|z| plus the probability below -|z|.
By symmetry that is 2 * (1 - norm_cdf(abs(z))).
z = (sample_mean - mu0) / (sd / math.sqrt(n)), then (round(z, 4), round(p_two_sided(z), 4)).

It is not the probability that the null is true, and 0.05 is a convention, not a law. A mean of 103 against 100 with 100 observations gives z = 2 and p = 0.046; a mean of 101 gives p = 0.5. The third test is the trap of large samples: a difference of 0.8 is highly significant with 400 observations, and may still be too small to matter.
