exercises.statement:
The median has no simple formula for its interval, so resample. Write bootstrap_median_ci(xs, n_boot, seed, level=0.95):

  1. Make rng = random.Random(seed).
  2. n_boot times: draw len(xs) values from xs with replacement using rng.choices(xs, k=len(xs)), and record the median of the draw (statistics.median).
  3. Sort the recorded medians. With a = (1 - level) / 2, the interval is the medians at positions int(a * n_boot) and int((1 - a) * n_boot) - 1.

Return (median of xs, low, high).
exercises.starter:
import random
import statistics


def bootstrap_median_ci(xs, n_boot, seed, level=0.95):
    pass

tests.test:
import random
r = random.Random(5)
xs = [round(r.gauss(0, 1), 3) for _ in range(30)]
print(bootstrap_median_ci([5, 5, 5, 5], 200, 9), tuple(round(v, 4) for v in bootstrap_median_ci(xs, 40, 4)))
print(bootstrap_median_ci([1, 2, 3, 100], 2000, 4, level=0.5))

a = bootstrap_median_ci(list(range(1, 102)), 400, 7)
b = bootstrap_median_ci(list(range(1, 102)), 400, 7)
print(a == b, a[0], a[1] < 51 < a[2])

hints: Use only rng for randomness, in the order described, so the result can be repeated exactly.
One loop builds the list of medians: [statistics.median(rng.choices(xs, k=n)) for _ in range(n_boot)].
After meds.sort(): low = meds[int(a * n_boot)], high = meds[int((1 - a) * n_boot) - 1], return (statistics.median(xs), low, high).
exercises.solution:
import random
import statistics


def bootstrap_median_ci(xs, n_boot, seed, level=0.95):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(xs)
    meds = sorted(statistics.median(rng.choices(xs, k=n)) for _ in range(n_boot))
    a = (1 - level) / 2
    return (statistics.median(xs), meds[int(a * n_boot)], meds[int((1 - a) * n_boot) - 1])
exercises.explanation: The bootstrap treats the sample as the population and asks how much a statistic would move between samples. It works for medians, ratios, AUC and any metric without a formula, which is why it is the workhorse of offline evaluation. This is the percentile method, the simplest; it is less reliable for small samples and statistics far from normal. Seeding the generator is what makes the analysis repeatable: the third test runs it twice and gets the same answer.

exercises.title: A permutation test
exercises.statement:
Did a new onboarding flow raise the amount customers deposit? Write perm_test(a, b, n_perm, seed): a two-sided test of whether the means of groups a and b differ.

  1. The observed statistic is abs(mean(b) - mean(a)).
  2. Pool the values as a + b. With rng = random.Random(seed), n_perm times: rng.shuffle(pooled), take the first len(a) as group A and the rest as group B, and compute the same statistic.
  3. Count the shuffles whose statistic is at least the observed one (allow 1e-12 for rounding). Return (observed rounded to 4, (count + 1) / (n_perm + 1) rounded to 4).
hints: Write a small mean helper, and the statistic as abs(mean(b) - mean(a)).
Shuffle a copy of the pooled list in place each time, then slice it: pooled[:len(a)] and pooled[len(a):].
if stat >= observed - 1e-12: count += 1. The + 1 on both sides counts the observed split as one of the permutations, so the p-value is never 0.
exercises.explanation: If the flow made no difference, the group labels are arbitrary, so shuffling them shows how big a difference chance alone produces. No assumption of normality is needed, only that the groups are exchangeable under the null. With five customers per group, a difference of 3.6 or more happens by chance in only about 1% of shuffles (p = 0.0125). Identical groups give a p-value of 1. Permutation tests are a good answer to 'my metric is skewed and my sample is small, how do I test it?', and they are how many experimentation platforms check results computed in other ways.

exercises.title: Two conversion rates: the z-test
exercises.statement:
A/B test: xa of na users converted with the old page and xb of nb with the new one. Using norm_cdf (given), write ab_test(xa, na, xb, nb) that returns (lift, z, p):

  • lift is pb - pa, the difference in conversion rate, rounded to 4 places;
  • z uses the pooled rate p = (xa + xb) / (na + nb) and the standard error sqrt(p (1 - p) (1 / na + 1 / nb)), rounded to 4;
  • p is the two-sided p-value, rounded to 4.
hints: Conversion rates first: pa = xa / na, pb = xb / nb.
Under the null hypothesis both groups share one rate, so estimate it from all users together: that is the pooled rate.
z = (pb - pa) / se, and the p-value is 2 * (1 - norm_cdf(abs(z))).
exercises.solution:
import math


def ab_test(xa, na, xb, nb):
    pa, pb = xa / na, xb / nb
    p = (xa + xb) / (na + nb)
    se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / na + 1 / nb))
    z = (pb - pa) / se
    pval = 2 * (1 - norm_cdf(abs(z)))
    return (round(pb - pa, 4), round(z, 4), round(pval, 4))
exercises.explanation: From 10% to 12.5% with 2,000 users per arm is z = 2.5, p = 0.012. Going from 10 to 13 conversions in 100 users, a 30% relative lift, is nowhere near significant (p = 0.51), while 10,300 against 10,000 in 100,000 users, a 3% lift, is p = 0.026: sample size decides what a test can see, the next exercise. A test answers 'is there a difference', so a negative lift is detected as readily as a positive one; deciding to ship needs the size of the lift and its interval, and the guardrail metrics that must not get worse.

exercises.title: How many users does a test need?
exercises.statement:
Before an A/B test, decide how many users each group needs to detect a given change. Write sample_size(p1, p2, z_alpha=1.959964, z_beta=0.841621), the users per group:

n = (z_alpha + z_beta) ** 2 * (p1 (1 - p1) + p2 (1 - p2)) / (p1 - p2) ** 2, rounded up to a whole number.

The default z-values are for a two-sided 5% significance level and 80% power. Also write days_needed(p1, p2, users_per_day): the whole days needed to fill both groups when traffic is split evenly.
hints: Translate the formula directly; math.ceil rounds up.
Halving the difference p1 - p2 multiplies the sample size by about four.
days_needed: both groups together need 2 * sample_size(p1, p2) users; divide by the daily users and round up.
exercises.explanation: Detecting 10% to 12% needs about 3,800 users per group; 10% to 11% needs about 14,700, four times as many for half the effect. Raising power from 80% to 90% (the second test) adds a third. Rare events are expensive: 2% to 2.4% needs more than 21,000 per group. This calculation, the minimum detectable effect it implies, and 'run full weeks to cover weekday patterns' are the first things an experimentation interviewer asks about. Stopping as soon as the p-value dips below 0.05 ('peeking') breaks the guarantee; fix the sample size first, or use a sequential method designed for it.

exercises.title: Sample ratio mismatch
exercises.statement:
A test meant to split users 50/50 got 50,600 and 49,400. Before reading any result, check the split. Write srm_p(n_a, n_b, expected_share_a=0.5):

  • the expected counts are N * share and N * (1 - share) with N = n_a + n_b;
  • the chi-square statistic is the sum over both groups of (observed - expected) ** 2 / expected;
  • with one degree of freedom the p-value is math.erfc(math.sqrt(chi2 / 2)).

Return (chi2, p), both rounded to 4 places.
hints: Compute the two expected counts from the total and the intended share.
The statistic adds one term per group. With one degree of freedom, chi-square is the square of a standard normal z, which is where erfc comes from.
chi2 = (n_a - ea) ** 2 / ea + (n_b - eb) ** 2 / eb, p = math.erfc(math.sqrt(chi2 / 2)).
exercises.explanation: A 50.6/49.4 split of 100,000 users looks harmless and has a p-value near 0.0001: something is dropping users from one group, a redirect that fails, a bot filter, a crash on one variant. Results from a test with a sample ratio mismatch cannot be trusted, however good they look, because the groups are no longer comparable. Large experimentation platforms run this check on every test automatically; mentioning it unprompted is one of the clearest signals of real experience in an A/B testing interview.

exercises.title: Many metrics at once: Holm's correction
exercises.statement:
A test looks at many metrics, and some will reach p < 0.05 by chance alone. Write holm(pvals, alpha=0.05): return a list of booleans, in the original order, saying which hypotheses are rejected by the Holm-Bonferroni method:

  1. Sort the p-values from smallest to largest (on a tie, keep the original order).
  2. Go through them in that order. The i-th smallest (counting from 0) is rejected if it is at most alpha / (m - i), where m is the number of p-values.
  3. Stop at the first one that is not rejected: it and every larger p-value are not rejected.

Also write bonferroni(pvals, alpha=0.05), which rejects each p-value at most alpha / m.

tests.expected_output: [True, False, False, True] [True, False, False, True]
[True, False, False, True, True] [False, False, False, True, False]

hints: Sort the indices by p-value: sorted(range(m), key=lambda i: (pvals[i], i)).
Walk the sorted indices with their position i. The threshold grows as you go: alpha / m, then alpha / (m - 1), and so on.
Start with [False] * m; set True for each index while the test passes, and break at the first failure.
exercises.explanation: With 20 independent metrics and no real effect, the chance that at least one reaches p < 0.05 is 64%. Bonferroni divides the threshold by the number of tests; Holm does the same for the smallest p-value and relaxes it step by step, so it never rejects less than Bonferroni and often more, with the same guarantee. In practice: name one primary metric before the test starts, treat the others as guardrails or exploration, and correct when you must claim several wins. Controlling the false discovery rate instead (Benjamini-Hochberg) is the answer when you screen hundreds of features or segments.

exercises.title: K-fold cross-validation, by hand
exercises.statement: Write kfold(n, k): split the indices 0 .. n - 1 into k folds of consecutive indices, as equal as possible, with the first n % k folds one larger. Return a list of k pairs (train, test): for each fold, test is that fold's indices and train is every other index, in increasing order.

tests.test:
for tr, te in kfold(10, 3):
    print(te, len(tr))

f = kfold(103, 5)
print([len(te) for _, te in f], sorted(i for _, te in f for i in te) == list(range(103)), all(set(tr).isdisjoint(te) for tr, te in f))

hints: Fold sizes: q, r = divmod(n, k); fold j has q + 1 indices if j < r, else q.
Walk a start index along the folds: each fold is list(range(start, start + size)).
Train for a fold is every index not in it: [i for i in range(n) if i < start or i >= start + size].
exercises.solution:
def kfold(n, k):
    q, r = divmod(n, k)
    out, start = [], 0
    for j in range(k):
        size = q + (1 if j < r else 0)
        test = list(range(start, start + size))
        train = [i for i in range(n) if i < start or i >= start + size]
        out.append((train, test))
        start += size
    return out
exercises.explanation: Each row is used for testing exactly once and for training k - 1 times, so every row counts and the score has less variance than one split. This is scikit-learn's KFold without shuffling. Consecutive folds are right only when the row order means nothing. If the rows are sorted by date or by class, shuffle first, stratify (next exercise), or, for time, never let the future train a model that predicts the past.

exercises.title: Missing values, learned from training data
exercises.statement: Write fit_impute(xs): the median of the values in a training column that are not None. Write apply_impute(xs, median): return (filled, flags), where filled replaces each None with the median and flags is 1 where the value was missing and 0 otherwise.

tests.test:
m = fit_impute([4, None, 1, 9, None, 3])
print(m, apply_impute([None, 5, None], m))

hints: statistics.median of [x for x in xs if x is not None].
Test with x is None, not not x: a real value of 0 is not missing.
filled = [median if x is None else x for x in xs], flags = [1 if x is None else 0 for x in xs].
exercises.explanation: The median resists outliers better than the mean, and the flag keeps the fact that a value was missing, which is often informative in itself (an income left blank on an application). The median is learned from training rows only and stored with the model, so new data are filled the same way, the same rule as for scaling. Tree models such as XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values themselves by learning which branch they go down, which is one reason they are the default for tabular data.

exercises.title: Stratified folds
exercises.statement:
When the positive class is rare, a random fold can end up with no positives at all. Write stratified_folds(labels, k): return a list fold with one entry per row, the fold number (0 to k - 1) that row belongs to.

Go through the classes in sorted order. Within each class, give its rows, in their original order, to folds 0, 1, 2, ... in turn, continuing the count from where the previous class stopped.

tests.test:
y = [1 if i % 10 == 0 else 0 for i in range(50)]
f = stratified_folds(y, 5)
print([sum(1 for i in range(50) if f[i] == j and y[i] == 1) for j in range(5)], [f.count(j) for j in range(5)])

hints: Group the row indices by class: a dictionary from label to the list of indices, built in one pass.
Keep one counter c across all classes. Each row gets c % k, then c += 1.
for label in sorted(by_class): for i in by_class[label]: fold[i] = c % k; c += 1.
exercises.explanation: Dealing each class out like cards gives every fold the same share of each class, give or take one, and fold sizes that differ by at most one. With 5 positives in 50 rows, each of 5 folds gets exactly one. Continuing the count across classes keeps the folds balanced in size too. For fraud, churn or default, where positives are 1 to 5 percent, stratified folds are the default, and the score to report is the mean and spread across folds.

exercises.title: Scaling without leakage
exercises.statement:
Standardising a feature uses its mean and standard deviation. If they are computed on all the data, the validation rows have leaked into training. Write fit_scaler(xs) that returns (mean, sd) of a training list (population standard deviation, dividing by n; use 1.0 if it is 0), and transform(xs, scaler) that returns (x - mean) / sd for each value.

Then write leak_gap(train, valid): the mean of the transformed validation values when the scaler is fitted on train only, minus the same when it is fitted on train + valid. Round to 4 places.

tests.test:
s = fit_scaler([2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0])
print(s, [round(v, 4) for v in transform([2.0, 5.0, 10.0], s)])

hints: fit only computes and returns numbers; transform only applies them. Keeping the two apart is the whole point.
Population standard deviation: math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / len(xs)).
leak_gap: honest = transform(valid, fit_scaler(train)), leaky = transform(valid, fit_scaler(train + valid)), then the difference of their means.
exercises.explanation: When validation data shift, as after a change in customer behaviour, the honestly scaled values sit far outside the training range (8.5 standard deviations above the mean here), and the model sees that. Fitted on everything, the same rows look ordinary (1.4), and the validation score hides the problem. This is why scikit-learn puts every fitted step in a Pipeline and refits it inside each fold: imputation, scaling, encoding and feature selection all learn from data, and all must learn from training rows only. 'Where can leakage come from?' is one of the most reliable ML interview questions; the answer starts here.

exercises.title: Target encoding without leakage
exercises.statement:
Target encoding replaces a category (a merchant, a city) by the average target for that category. Computed on the same rows it is used for, it leaks the target. Write oof_target_encode(cats, ys, folds, m=10):

  • folds[i] is the fold of row i. For each row, use only the rows of other folds.
  • From those rows: prior is the mean of ys; for the row's category, n is how many there are and s the sum of their ys.
  • The encoding is the smoothed mean (s + m * prior) / (n + m), rounded to 4 places. A category not seen in the other folds gets the prior.

Return the list of encodings, one per row.
exercises.starter:
def oof_target_encode(cats, ys, folds, m=10):
    pass

tests.test:
cats = ['a', 'a', 'b', 'b', 'a', 'b']
ys = [1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0]
print(oof_target_encode(cats, ys, [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1], m=0), oof_target_encode(cats, ys, [0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1], m=2))

cats = ['rare'] + ['common'] * 9
ys = [1] + [0] * 9
f = [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0]
print(oof_target_encode(cats, ys, f, m=0)[0], oof_target_encode(cats, ys, f, m=5)[:4])

hints: For row i, the usable rows are [j for j in range(len(cats)) if folds[j] != folds[i]].
From those, the prior uses every usable row; n and s use only the usable rows with cats[j] == cats[i].
enc = (s + m * prior) / (n + m); when n + m is 0 (an unseen category with m = 0), use prior.
exercises.solution:
def oof_target_encode(cats, ys, folds, m=10):
    out = []
    for i in range(len(cats)):
        rows = [j for j in range(len(cats)) if folds[j] != folds[i]]
        prior = sum(ys[j] for j in rows) / len(rows)
        same = [ys[j] for j in rows if cats[j] == cats[i]]
        n, s = len(same), sum(same)
        enc = (s + m * prior) / (n + m) if n + m > 0 else prior
        out.append(round(enc, 4))
    return out
exercises.explanation: Encoding each row from the other folds means no row ever sees its own target, so the feature looks as informative in training as it will be on new data. Smoothing pulls small categories toward the overall rate: a merchant seen once with a fraud would otherwise get an encoding of 1.0. In the last test the rare category is unseen outside its own fold and correctly falls back to the prior. Grandmasters use this, with frequency encoding and group statistics, on nearly every tabular competition, including the card-fraud replay; scikit-learn has it as TargetEncoder, which does the cross-fitting for you.

exercises.title: ROC-AUC from ranks
exercises.statement:
ROC-AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, counting ties as half. Write roc_auc(labels, scores) (labels are 0 or 1) by comparing every positive with every negative.

Return 0.5 if there are no positives or no negatives.

tests.test:
import random
r = random.Random(2)
y = [r.random() < 0.3 for _ in range(300)]
s = [r.random() + (0.5 if v else 0) for v in y]
a = roc_auc([int(v) for v in y], s)
print(round(a, 4), roc_auc([int(v) for v in y], [-x for x in s]) == round(1 - a, 12) or abs(roc_auc([int(v) for v in y], [-x for x in s]) - (1 - a)) < 1e-12)

hints: Split the scores into the positives' and the negatives'.
For every pair (positive, negative): 1 if the positive scores higher, 0.5 if they are equal, 0 otherwise.
Divide the total by len(pos) * len(neg). This takes time proportional to their product, fine for a few thousand rows.
exercises.explanation: AUC depends only on the order of the scores, not their values, which is why it was the metric of the card-fraud competition and why it says nothing about whether the probabilities are calibrated. It is the Mann-Whitney statistic; sorting once gives an n log n version, which is what libraries do. AUC 0.5 is a coin, 1.0 a perfect ranking, and an AUC below 0.5 means the scores are upside down. For rare positives, also look at precision and recall at the threshold you will use, or the precision-recall curve: an AUC of 0.95 can still mean most alerts are false.

exercises.title: Log loss and the Brier score
exercises.statement:
AUC judges the order of the scores. When the numbers themselves are used as probabilities (for pricing or expected loss), judge them as probabilities. Write:

  • log_loss(labels, probs, eps=1e-15): the mean of -(y log(p) + (1 - y) log(1 - p)), with each p first clipped into [eps, 1 - eps].
  • brier(labels, probs): the mean of (p - y) ** 2.
hints: Clip first: p = min(max(p, eps), 1 - eps), so that log(0) never happens.
Only one of the two terms is non-zero for each row: log(p) for a positive, log(1 - p) for a negative.
Average with sum(...) / len(labels) in both functions.
exercises.explanation: Log loss punishes confident mistakes without limit: a probability of 0 for something that happened costs 34.5 here, only because of the clipping, and infinity without it. Brier is bounded and gentler. Always predicting 0.5 gives a log loss of 0.693 and a Brier score of 0.25, the baselines to beat. A model can have a high AUC and poor log loss when it ranks well but its probabilities are off; calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression, fitted on held-out data) fixes the numbers without changing the order.

exercises.title: Choosing a threshold by cost
exercises.statement: A model gives each transaction a score; you block those at or above a threshold. A missed fraud costs cost_fn and blocking an honest transaction costs cost_fp. Write best_threshold(labels, scores, cost_fp, cost_fn): try every distinct score as the threshold, plus inf (block nothing). Return (threshold, total_cost) for the cheapest; on a tie, the higher threshold.
exercises.starter:
def best_threshold(labels, scores, cost_fp, cost_fn):
    pass
hints: For a threshold t, a false positive is a negative with score >= t; a false negative is a positive with score < t.
The candidates are sorted(set(scores)) + [float('inf')]. Compute the cost of each.
Keep the best as you go; replace it when a candidate is cheaper, or equally cheap and higher (<= while walking up the sorted candidates).
exercises.explanation: The right threshold is a business decision, not 0.5: when a missed fraud costs ten times a blocked customer, the cheapest rule blocks generously; when the costs reverse, it blocks almost nothing. Interviewers want to hear that the model ranks and the costs choose the cut, and that the costs should come from the business (chargebacks, review time, customers lost to false declines). With calibrated probabilities the optimum has a closed form, block when p > cost_fp / (cost_fp + cost_fn); searching the scores, as here, works whether or not they are calibrated.

exercises.title: Weight of evidence and information value
exercises.statement:
Credit-risk teams describe a binned feature (say, income bands) by its weight of evidence. For each bin, with good and bad counts:

  • dist_good = good / total good and dist_bad = bad / total bad, over all bins;
  • WoE = ln(dist_good / dist_bad);
  • the feature's information value is the sum over bins of (dist_good - dist_bad) * WoE.

Write woe_iv(bins): bins is a list of (name, good, bad). To avoid dividing by zero, add 0.5 to every bin's good and bad before computing anything. Return ([(name, WoE rounded to 4), ...], IV rounded to 4).
hints: Add 0.5 to every count first, then total the goods and the bads.
Each bin's WoE compares its share of all goods with its share of all bads; positive means safer than average.
iv = sum((dg - db) * woe for ...); build the list of (name, round(woe, 4)) in the input order.
exercises.solution:
import math


def woe_iv(bins):
    adj = [(name, g + 0.5, b + 0.5) for name, g, b in bins]
    tg = sum(g for _, g, _ in adj)
    tb = sum(b for _, _, b in adj)
    out, iv = [], 0.0
    for name, g, b in adj:
        dg, db = g / tg, b / tb
        woe = math.log(dg / db)
        out.append((name, round(woe, 4)))
        iv += (dg - db) * woe
    return (out, round(iv, 4))
exercises.explanation: WoE turns each bin into a number on the log-odds scale, which is why scorecards built with logistic regression on WoE features are still standard in banking: monotonic, explainable to a regulator, and robust to outliers. Rules of thumb for IV: below 0.02 useless, 0.1 to 0.3 medium, above 0.3 strong, and above 0.5 suspiciously strong, often a sign of leakage. Two bins with identical rates carry no information: IV 0. In a bank interview, expect to be asked how you would bin a variable, why you would merge bins until WoE is monotonic, and what IV says that a correlation does not.

exercises.title: Amdahl's law
exercises.statement:
A fraction f of a program's work can be shared out perfectly among processors. The rest runs on one processor however many there are.

Write three functions.

  • amdahl(f, p) returns the speedup on p processors: 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p).
  • amdahl_limit(f) returns the speedup that no number of processors can pass: 1 / (1 - f). When f is 1 there is no limit, so return float('inf').
  • efficiency(f, p) returns the speedup divided by p: how much of each processor is doing useful work.
hints: Write the time on p processors as a fraction of the time on one: the serial part stays 1 - f, the parallel part becomes f / p.
Speedup is old time over new time, so 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p). For the limit, let p grow until f / p vanishes.
amdahl_limit: if f == 1: return float('inf'), otherwise 1 / (1 - f). efficiency is amdahl(f, p) / p.
exercises.explanation: With 90% of the work parallel, ten processors give a speedup of 5.3, and a thousand could not give 10. The serial tenth sets the ceiling. Efficiency shows the same thing from the other side: at 100 processors and 99% parallel work, half of every processor is wasted. Gustafson's answer is that people use more processors to solve bigger problems, where the parallel part grows and the serial part does not.

exercises.title: Sharing a loop among threads
exercises.statement:
A loop has n iterations, numbered from 0, and p threads share them. Each thread takes one unbroken run of iterations, in thread order, and the runs are as equal as they can be: when n is not a multiple of p, the first n % p threads take one extra.

Write block_range(n, p, k). It returns (start, end) for thread k: the thread runs iterations start up to, but not including, end.

tests.test: print([block_range(10, 3, k) for k in range(3)])
print([block_range(8, 4, k) for k in range(4)], [block_range(3, 5, k) for k in range(5)])

hints: Every thread gets at least n // p iterations. How many are left over, and who gets them?
Thread k starts after all the threads before it. Each of those took n // p, and the first n % p of them took one more.
q, r = divmod(n, p). start = k * q + min(k, r). end = start + q + (1 if k < r else 0).
exercises.explanation: This is what OpenMP's static schedule does with a for loop, and what an MPI program does by hand when it gives each process its slice of an array. min(k, r) counts how many of the earlier threads took an extra iteration. The formula needs no loop, so every process can work out its own slice without being told.

exercises.title: A direct-mapped cache
exercises.statement:
A cache has lines lines. Each line holds one block of block_size bytes of memory.

  • The byte at address a belongs to block number a // block_size.
  • A block can live in only one line: line number block % lines.
  • Reading an address is a hit if its block is already in its line. Otherwise it is a miss, and the block replaces whatever that line held.

Write cache_misses(addresses, lines, block_size). The cache starts empty. Return the number of misses for the addresses read in the order given.
hints: Keep a list with one entry per line that remembers which block the line holds. None means empty.
For each address work out the block, then the line. Compare the block with what the line holds.
block = a // block_size, line = block % lines. If held[line] != block: count a miss and store block in held[line].
exercises.explanation: Reading memory in order costs one miss per block, because the neighbours arrive with the first byte. That is spatial locality. The second test shows the weakness of direct mapping: addresses 0 and 64 fight over one line and every read misses, although three lines stand empty. Real caches soften this by letting a block choose among a few lines, which is called set-associative.

exercises.title: Row order against column order
exercises.statement:
A matrix of rows by cols numbers is stored row after row from address 0. Each number takes 8 bytes, so the element in row r and column c is at address (r * cols + c) * 8.

Write traversal_misses(rows, cols, order, lines, block_size). It returns the number of cache misses when every element is read once through a direct-mapped cache with lines lines of block_size bytes, starting empty.

  • When order is "row", read row 0 from left to right, then row 1, and so on.
  • When order is "col", read column 0 from top to bottom, then column 1, and so on.

The cache works as in the exercise before: block a // block_size lives in line block % lines.
exercises.starter:
def traversal_misses(rows, cols, order, lines, block_size):
    pass
hints: Two steps: produce the addresses in the order they are read, then count the misses as you did before.
The two orders differ only in which loop is outside. For "col" the column loop is outside and the row loop is inside.
Build addresses with two nested loops and (r * cols + c) * 8, then run the cache: held = [None] * lines, a miss when held[block % lines] != block.
exercises.explanation: For a 64 by 64 matrix the row walk misses 512 times, once per block. The column walk misses on all 4096 reads, because each step jumps a whole row ahead and lands in a different block. Same data, same number of reads, eight times the misses. The middle test shows when the order stops mattering: when the cache can hold the whole matrix. This is why the loop order of a matrix product matters, and why NumPy asks whether an array is C-ordered.

exercises.title: Which element is mine?
exercises.statement:
A launch creates a grid of blocks, and each block holds the same number of threads. Every thread runs the same function and has to work out which element it is responsible for.

Write two functions.

  • global_index(t) returns the position of thread t in a one-dimensional launch: its block number times the number of threads in a block, plus its own number inside the block. Use t.blockIdx.x, t.blockDim.x and t.threadIdx.x.
  • blocks_needed(n, block_size) returns the smallest number of blocks of block_size threads that gives each of n elements a thread of its own.

tests.test:
a = Thread(Dim(0, 0), Dim(0, 0), Dim(256, 1), Dim(4, 1))
b = Thread(Dim(2, 0), Dim(5, 0), Dim(256, 1), Dim(4, 1))
c = Thread(Dim(3, 0), Dim(255, 0), Dim(256, 1), Dim(4, 1))
print(global_index(a), global_index(b), global_index(c))

hints: Block 0 owns elements 0 to blockDim.x - 1. Where does block 1 start?
The threads of block b start at b * blockDim.x. Add the thread's own number.
For the blocks: divide and round up. With whole numbers that is (n + block_size - 1) // block_size.
exercises.explanation:
These two lines open almost every CUDA program. In CUDA C they read:

int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
int blocks = (n + blockSize - 1) / blockSize;

Rounding up means the last block usually has threads with no element to work on. The next exercise deals with them.

import random
from collections import namedtuple

Dim = namedtuple("Dim", "x y")
Thread = namedtuple("Thread", "blockIdx threadIdx blockDim gridDim")


def launch(kernel, grid, block, *args):
    """Run kernel once for every thread, in a shuffled order.

    In CUDA C this is kernel<<<grid, block>>>(args).
    grid is (blocks in x, blocks in y).
    block is (threads in x, threads in y).
    A GPU promises no order, so neither does this.
    """
    grid, block = Dim(*grid), Dim(*block)
    ids = [(bx, by, tx, ty)
           for by in range(grid.y) for bx in range(grid.x)
           for ty in range(block.y) for tx in range(block.x)]
    random.Random(len(ids)).shuffle(ids)
    for bx, by, tx, ty in ids:
        t = Thread(Dim(bx, by), Dim(tx, ty), block, grid)
        kernel(t, *args)

exercises.title: A first kernel: a times x plus y
exercises.statement:
Write the kernel saxpy(t, n, a, x, y). Each thread handles one element: it replaces y[i] with a * x[i] + y[i], where i is the thread's global index.

The launch rounds the number of threads up to whole blocks, so there may be more threads than elements. A thread whose index is n or more must do nothing.

A kernel returns nothing. Its result is what it writes into y.
exercises.starter:
def saxpy(t, n, a, x, y):
    pass

tests.test:
n = 1000
x = list(range(n))
y = [1] * n
launch(saxpy, (16, 1), (64, 1), n, 2, x, y)
print(sum(y), y[0], y[999], x[999])

hints: Start with the line from the exercise before: i = t.blockIdx.x * t.blockDim.x + t.threadIdx.x.
There is no loop in a kernel. The launch is the loop: each call does the work of one iteration.
if i < n: then y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]. Compare with n, not with the length of the list.
exercises.explanation:
The same kernel in CUDA C, and the line that launches it:

__global__ void saxpy(int n, float a, const float *x, float *y) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i < n) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}

saxpy<<<(n + 255) / 256, 256>>>(n, 2.0f, d_x, d_y);

The loop of the CPU version has gone into the launch. The guard i < n is what stops the spare threads of the last block from writing past the end of the array, which on a real GPU corrupts memory without any error message. Each thread writes only its own y[i], so the order the threads run in cannot matter.

exercises.title: Two dimensions: transpose
exercises.statement:
A matrix with rows rows and cols columns is stored as one flat list, row after row: the element in row r, column c is at r * cols + c.

Write the kernel transpose(t, rows, cols, src, dst). The launch is two-dimensional. A thread's column is its global index in x, and its row is its global index in y. The thread at row r, column c copies that element of src to row c, column r of dst. dst has cols rows and rows columns, stored the same way.

The launch may cover more rows and columns than the matrix has. Threads outside the matrix must do nothing.

def transpose(t, rows, cols, src, dst):
    pass

dst = [0] * 6
launch(transpose, (2, 2), (2, 2), 2, 3, src, dst)
print(dst)

dst = [None] * 12

Check both: r < rows and c < cols. A flat index that happens to be in range is not enough, because column 5 of a 4-column matrix lands in the next row.
Reading: src[r * cols + c]. Writing: dst has rows columns, so row c, column r is at c * rows + r.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C:

__global__ void transpose(int rows, int cols, const float *src, float *dst) {
    int c = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    int r = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    if (r < rows && c < cols) dst[c * rows + r] = src[r * cols + c];
}

dim3 block(16, 16);
dim3 grid((cols + 15) / 16, (rows + 15) / 16);
transpose<<<grid, block>>>(rows, cols, d_src, d_dst);

The GPU only knows flat memory. Rows and columns are your arithmetic, and the two lists use different arithmetic because their widths differ. Checking the row and the column separately matters: a thread in a column past the edge would otherwise read the start of the next row.

exercises.title: Reading neighbours: a blur
exercises.statement:
Write the kernel blur(t, n, src, dst). For an element with a neighbour on each side, dst[i] becomes the mean of src[i - 1], src[i] and src[i + 1]. The first and the last element are copied unchanged. Threads past the end do nothing.

Then write the host function smooth(values, steps, block_size). It applies the blur steps times and returns the result as a new list, leaving values as it was. It calls launch(blur, (blocks, 1), (block_size, 1), n, a, b) once per step with enough blocks to cover the list.

Every thread must see the values from before the step, so each step reads from one list and writes to another, and the two swap roles for the next step.

tests.test:
src = [0, 0, 9, 0, 0, 6]
dst = [None] * 6
launch(blur, (2, 1), (4, 1), 6, src, dst)
print(dst, src)

d = [1, 5, 3, 8, 2, 7, 4, 6]
print([round(v, 3) for v in smooth(d, 3, 3)], d, smooth([4], 5, 2), smooth([], 2, 2), smooth(d, 0, 4))

hints: The kernel: compute i, return if i >= n. The ends are i == 0 and i == n - 1.
The host: a = list(values), b = [0] * n. After each launch, swap: a, b = b, a.
After the last swap the newest values are in a, so return a. If you launched with the same list for reading and writing, some threads would read values already changed in this step.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C the kernel is:

__global__ void blur(int n, const float *src, float *dst) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i >= n) return;
    if (i == 0 || i == n - 1) dst[i] = src[i];
    else dst[i] = (src[i - 1] + src[i] + src[i + 1]) / 3.0f;
}

and the host swaps two device pointers between launches. A kernel that read and wrote the same array would give a different picture on every run, because a thread might read a neighbour before or after that neighbour was updated. Two buffers make the result the same whatever the order. Every stencil, from image filters to the finite-difference solvers of a numerical methods course, is built this way.

exercises.title: One thread per output: matrix product
exercises.statement:
a, b and c are n by n matrices stored as flat lists, row after row.

Write the kernel matmul(t, n, a, b, c). The launch is two-dimensional: a thread's column is its global index in x and its row is its global index in y. The thread at row r, column col computes one element of the product: the sum over k of a[r][k] * b[k][col], and stores it in c. Threads outside the matrix do nothing.
exercises.starter:
def matmul(t, n, a, b, c):
    pass

tests.test:
n = 5
eye = [1 if i // n == i % n else 0 for i in range(n * n)]
m = list(range(n * n))
c = [None] * (n * n)
launch(matmul, (3, 3), (2, 2), n, m, eye, c)
print(c == m, m[7])

hints: This kernel does contain a loop, over k. What disappears into the launch are the two outer loops, over rows and columns.
Row r of a starts at r * n. Column col of b is every n-th element starting at col.
total = 0, then for each k: total += a[r * n + k] * b[k * n + col]. Store it in c[r * n + col], inside if r < n and col < n:.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C:

__global__ void matmul(int n, const float *a, const float *b, float *c) {
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    if (row < n && col < n) {
        float total = 0.0f;
        for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) total += a[row * n + k] * b[k * n + col];
        c[row * n + col] = total;
    }
}

This is the plain version: n² threads, each doing n multiplications. Its weakness is the walk down a column of b, which jumps n elements at a time, the cache problem from the first lesson again. The faster version loads tiles of a and b into the block's shared memory first. That is the matrix product worth writing on the V100, and it is on the Syllabus list.

exercises.title: A sum without a shared total
exercises.statement:
A thousand threads cannot all add into one variable: each reads the old total, adds its value and writes back, and most of the additions are lost. A sum is built in rounds instead.

In the round with stride s, the thread at index i adds data[i + s] into data[i], but only when i is a multiple of 2 * s and i + s < n. After the rounds with stride 1, 2, 4 and so on, the total is in data[0].

Write the kernel reduce_step(t, n, stride, data).

Then write the host function gpu_sum(values, block_size). It copies values, calls launch(reduce_step, (blocks, 1), (block_size, 1), n, stride, data) once per round while the stride is less than n, and returns the total. It returns 0 for an empty list and leaves values as it was.

tests.test:

launch(reduce_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 1, d)
print(d)
launch(reduce_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 2, d)
print(d)
launch(reduce_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 4, d)
print(d)

v = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
print(gpu_sum(v, 4), gpu_sum(list(range(1, 14)), 4), gpu_sum([], 4), gpu_sum([5], 4), v)

seen = []
_launch = launch


def launch(kernel, grid, block, *args):
    seen.append(args[1])
    _launch(kernel, grid, block, *args)


print(gpu_sum(list(range(100)), 16), seen)

hints: The kernel is three lines: the index, one condition with two parts, one addition.
if i % (2 * stride) == 0 and i + stride < n: then data[i] += data[i + stride].
The host: data = list(values), stride = 1, then while stride < n: launch and double the stride. Return data[0], after handling the empty list.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C the kernel is:

__global__ void reduce_step(int n, int stride, float *data) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i % (2 * stride) == 0 && i + stride < n) data[i] += data[i + stride];
}

A hundred numbers take 7 rounds instead of 99 additions in a row: the depth is log n. No two threads touch the same element in a round, because the thread at i reads i + stride, and i + stride is never a multiple of 2 * stride, so no thread writes it. That is why the shuffled order cannot change the answer.

Real code does the rounds inside each block with shared memory and one launch, or calls atomicAdd, or uses a library. The idea of pairing up in a tree is the same in all of them, and it is how MPI_Reduce and an OpenMP reduction clause work as well.

exercises.title: Running totals in log n rounds
exercises.statement:
The running totals of [3, 1, 4, 1] are [3, 4, 8, 9]. On one processor that is a loop that carries a total, which looks impossible to share out. It can be done in rounds.

In the round with offset k, every element becomes itself plus the element k places to its left, if there is one:

  • dst[i] = src[i] + src[i - k] when i >= k
  • dst[i] = src[i] otherwise

Offsets double each round: 1, 2, 4, and so on while the offset is less than n. Every thread reads the values from before the round, so a round reads one list and writes another.

Write the kernel scan_step(t, n, offset, src, dst) and the host function gpu_running_totals(values, block_size), which launches launch(scan_step, (blocks, 1), (block_size, 1), n, offset, a, b) once per round and returns the running totals as a new list.

The host is the blur's host again: two lists, launch, swap. Only the stopping rule differs: while offset < n, doubling the offset.
After round 1 each element holds a sum of 2 neighbours, after round 2 a sum of 4, then 8. When the reach passes the start of the list the element is finished.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C the kernel is:

__global__ void scan_step(int n, int offset, const float *src, float *dst) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i >= n) return;
    dst[i] = (i >= offset) ? src[i] + src[i - offset] : src[i];
}

This is the Hillis and Steele scan. It finishes in log n rounds but does about n log n additions in total, more than the n − 1 of the simple loop: it buys speed with extra work. The PRAM model in your syllabus is where that trade is measured, as time against total work. Scans turn up wherever threads need to know where to write: compacting an array, building a histogram, sorting.

exercises.title: Word count
exercises.statement:
A MapReduce job is two functions.

  • mapper(record) looks at one record and returns a list of (key, value) pairs.
  • reducer(key, values) gets one key with the list of all the values that were paired with it, and returns one result.

The framework does the rest: it spreads the records over workers, gathers the pairs by key, and calls the reducer once per key.

Write mapper(line) and reducer(word, counts) so that the job counts how often each word appears. A word is whatever split() gives, in lower case. The mapper returns (word, 1) for every word in the line. The reducer returns (word, total).

tests.test:
lines = ['the cat sat', 'The dog sat', 'the end', '']
print(map_reduce(lines, mapper, reducer))

lines = ['a b a', 'b a', 'a a a c', 'c b', 'a']
print(map_reduce(lines, mapper, reducer, combiner=lambda word, counts: [reducer(word, counts)]))

hints: The mapper does not count anything. It only says: here is this word, once.
[(word, 1) for word in line.lower().split()].
The reducer adds the values up: (word, sum(counts)). Counting how many values there are would be wrong as soon as a worker has added some of them together already.
exercises.explanation: The third test puts the reducer to work as a combiner: each worker adds up its own pairs before sending them on, so ('a', 1) five times travels as ('a', 5) once. That only works because the reducer sums the values. One that returned len(counts) would pass the second test and fail the third. A combiner is safe when the operation gives the same answer however the values are grouped, which is true of sums, minimums and maximums.

exercises.title: A mean that survives a combiner
exercises.statement:
The records are (sensor, reading) pairs. The job must return each sensor's mean reading as (sensor, mean).

Each worker runs the combiner on the readings it happens to hold, so one sensor's readings reach the reducer already combined in uneven groups. A mean of those groups' means would be wrong. Carry a sum and a count instead.

Write three functions.

  • mapper(record) returns [(sensor, (reading, 1))].
  • combiner(sensor, values) gets a list of (sum, count) pairs and returns [(sensor, (total sum, total count))].
  • reducer(sensor, values) gets a list of (sum, count) pairs and returns (sensor, mean).

print(map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer, combiner), map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer))

print(map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer, combiner, workers=4))

hints: The value that travels is a pair. The mapper makes the smallest such pair: one reading, counted once.
The combiner and the reducer both start the same way: add up the first parts, add up the second parts.
total = sum(s for s, c in values), count = sum(c for s, c in values). The combiner returns [(sensor, (total, count))]; the reducer returns (sensor, total / count).
exercises.explanation: The mean of [0, 0, 100] is 33.3, but the mean of the means of [0, 0] and [100] is 50. A mean cannot be combined piece by piece; a sum and a count can. Federated averaging has exactly this shape: each client sends its update together with the number of samples behind it, and the server divides once at the end. Weighting clients by sample count is the combiner done properly.

exercises.title: Who sends to whom in a tree sum
exercises.statement:
p processes, ranked 0 to p - 1, each hold one number. They want the total at rank 0. If every process sent straight to rank 0, rank 0 would receive p - 1 messages one after another. A tree does it in about log p rounds.

In the round with step s, starting at 1 and doubling, every rank r that is an odd multiple of s sends what it holds to rank r - s, which adds it to its own. A rank that has sent takes no further part.

Write reduce_rounds(p). It returns a list with one entry per round; each entry is the list of (sender, receiver) pairs of that round, in ascending order of sender. Stop when only rank 0 still holds a value.

tests.test:
r = reduce_rounds(1000)
print(len(r), sum(len(x) for x in r), r[-1])

hints: In round 1 the senders are 1, 3, 5, ... In round 2 they are 2, 6, 10, ... What is the gap between senders in the round with step s?
The senders of a round are s, 3s, 5s, ...: range(s, p, 2 * s). Each sends to itself minus s.
rounds = [], s = 1, then while s < p: append [(r, r - s) for r in range(s, p, 2 * s)] and double s.
exercises.solution:
def reduce_rounds(p):
    rounds = []
    s = 1
    while s < p:
        rounds.append([(r, r - s) for r in range(s, p, 2 * s)])
        s *= 2
    return rounds
exercises.explanation: A thousand processes need 999 messages either way, but the tree spreads them over 10 rounds in which many pairs talk at once. This is what MPI_Reduce does inside, and it is the same pairing as the GPU sum: stride there, step here. In an MPI program each rank runs the same code and decides from its own rank and the step whether to call MPI_Send or MPI_Recv in this round.

exercises.title: Bisection
exercises.statement:
f is a continuous function, and f(lo) and f(hi) have opposite signs, so f is zero somewhere between them.

Write bisect_root(f, lo, hi, tol). Repeat while hi - lo is greater than tol: take the midpoint; if f is exactly zero there, return it; otherwise keep the half in which the sign still changes. At the end return the midpoint of what is left.
exercises.starter:
def bisect_root(f, lo, hi, tol):
    pass

tests.test:
import math
print(round(bisect_root(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, 0, 1, 1e-7), 5), round(bisect_root(lambda x: 3 - x, 0, 10, 1e-7), 5))

calls = []
def f(x):
    calls.append(x)
    return x ** 3 - 5
root = bisect_root(f, 0, 4, 0.01)
print(round(root, 2), len(calls) < 25, bisect_root(lambda x: x - 2, 0, 4, 1e-9))

hints: Compare the sign at the midpoint with the sign at lo. If they are the same, the root is in the upper half.
Two values have the same sign when their product is positive. Evaluate f(lo) once and keep it.
mid = (lo + hi) / 2, fm = f(mid). If fm == 0 return mid. If f_lo * fm > 0: lo, f_lo = mid, fm; else hi = mid. After the loop return (lo + hi) / 2.
exercises.explanation: Each step halves the interval, so the error after k steps is at most the starting width divided by 2ᵏ. That is slow, one binary digit per step, but it cannot fail: the root never leaves the bracket. It is binary search on a continuous function, and the same idea as the binary search exercises under DSA.

exercises.title: Newton's method
exercises.statement:
Newton's method improves a guess x for a root of f by following the tangent line at x down to zero: the new guess is x - f(x) / df(x), where df is the derivative of f.

Write newton(f, df, x0, steps). Start from x0, apply the update steps times, and return the result.
exercises.starter:
def newton(f, df, x0, steps):
    pass

tests.test:
f = lambda x: x * x - 2
df = lambda x: 2 * x
print([round(newton(f, df, 1.0, k), 6) for k in range(5)])
print(round(newton(lambda x: x ** 3 - 27, lambda x: 3 * x * x, 2.0, 8), 6), newton(lambda x: 2 * x - 6, lambda x: 2, 100.0, 1))

import math
print(round(newton(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, lambda x: -math.sin(x) - 1, 1.0, 5), 6))

hints: It is a loop that runs steps times and changes one variable.
Inside the loop: x = x - f(x) / df(x).
With steps equal to 0 the loop does not run and the function returns x0 itself.
exercises.explanation: Look at the first test: 1.5, then 1.4167, then 1.414216. The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step, which is called quadratic convergence. Bisection needs about 23 steps for the accuracy Newton reaches in 4. The price is that Newton needs the derivative and a starting guess near the root: where the derivative is close to zero the tangent is nearly flat and the next guess flies far away. The secant method replaces df with the slope between the last two guesses.

exercises.title: Slopes from function values
exercises.statement:
When only the values of f are available, a slope has to be estimated from them.

Write two functions.

  • forward_diff(f, x, h) returns (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h.
  • central_diff(f, x, h) returns (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h).

tests.test:
f = lambda x: x ** 3
print(round(forward_diff(f, 2, 0.01), 4), round(central_diff(f, 2, 0.01), 4))

import math
print(round(central_diff(math.sin, 0, 0.1), 5), round(forward_diff(math.sin, 0, 0.1), 5), central_diff(lambda x: 5 * x + 1, 3, 0.5))

f = lambda x: x * x
print([round(abs(forward_diff(f, 1, h) - 2), 6) for h in (0.1, 0.01)], [round(abs(central_diff(lambda x: x ** 3, 1, h) - 3), 6) for h in (0.1, 0.01)])

hints: Both are one line each. They are the slope of a straight line through two points on the curve.
Forward uses the points at x and x + h. Central uses x - h and x + h, which are 2 * h apart.
Mind the brackets in the denominator: / (2 * h), not / 2 * h.
exercises.explanation: The last test is the lesson. Making h ten times smaller makes the forward error ten times smaller, and the central error a hundred times smaller: forward is first order, central is second order. The central difference is what a gradient check uses in Stage 1 of the build, to confirm a hand-derived gradient. h cannot shrink for ever: below about 1e-8 for the forward form, rounding in f(x + h) - f(x) grows faster than the formula's own error falls.

exercises.title: The trapezoidal rule
exercises.statement:
To estimate the area under f between a and b, cut the interval into n strips of equal width h and treat each strip as a trapezoid. Added up, that is

h * (f(x0) / 2 + f(x1) + f(x2) + ... + f(x_{n-1}) + f(xn) / 2)

where x0 = a, xn = b and the points are h apart.

Write trapezoid(f, a, b, n).
exercises.starter:
def trapezoid(f, a, b, n):
    pass

tests.test: print(trapezoid(lambda x: x * x, 0, 1, 4), trapezoid(lambda x: 2 * x + 1, 0, 3, 1))

f = lambda x: x * x
print([round(abs(trapezoid(f, 0, 3, n) - 9), 6) for n in (10, 20, 40)])

hints: h = (b - a) / n. The points are a + i * h for i from 0 to n.
The two end values count half, every value in between counts in full.
total = (f(a) + f(b)) / 2, then add f(a + i * h) for i in range(1, n), then return h * total.
exercises.explanation: The last test doubles the strips twice, and the error falls by four each time: 0.045, 0.01125, 0.0028. The error is proportional to h², second order. Romberg integration uses exactly that regularity: it combines the results for n and 2n so that the h² terms cancel. The rule is also the standard first MPI program: each process integrates its own slice of the interval and the slices are added with MPI_Reduce.

exercises.title: Simpson's rule
exercises.statement:
Simpson's rule fits a parabola through each pair of strips instead of a straight line through each strip. With n strips of width h, where n is even:

h / 3 * (f(x0) + 4 * f(x1) + 2 * f(x2) + 4 * f(x3) + ... + 4 * f(x_{n-1}) + f(xn))

The inner points take the weights 4, 2, 4, 2, ..., 4: 4 at odd positions, 2 at even ones.

Write simpson(f, a, b, n). n is always even.
exercises.starter:
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    pass

tests.test: print(round(simpson(lambda x: x ** 3, 0, 2, 2), 6), round(simpson(lambda x: x ** 4, 0, 1, 4), 6))

f = lambda x: x ** 4
print([round(abs(simpson(f, 0, 2, n) - 6.4) * 1e4, 3) for n in (4, 8, 16)])

hints: h = (b - a) / n. Start the total with the two end values.
Loop i from 1 to n - 1. The weight is 4 when i is odd and 2 when it is even.
total += (4 if i % 2 else 2) * f(a + i * h), and at the end return h / 3 * total.
exercises.explanation: The first test integrates x³ exactly with two strips, although a parabola cannot follow a cubic: the errors on the two sides cancel. Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials up to degree 3 and its error is proportional to h⁴, so doubling the strips divides the error by 16, as the last test shows. Ten strips give sin to four decimal places where the trapezoidal rule needed a hundred for three.

exercises.title: The polynomial through given points
exercises.statement:
Through n points with different x values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n - 1. Lagrange's form writes it without solving any equations:

P(x) = sum over i of ys[i] * L_i(x)

where L_i(x) is the product, over every j other than i, of (x - xs[j]) / (xs[i] - xs[j]). Each L_i is 1 at xs[i] and 0 at every other given point.

Write lagrange(xs, ys, x). It returns the value of that polynomial at x.

tests.test:
import math
xs = [0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]
print(round(lagrange(xs, [math.sin(v) for v in xs], 0.75), 4), round(math.sin(0.75), 4), round(lagrange([-1, 0, 1], [1, 0, 1], 3), 6))

hints: Two nested loops: the outer one adds the terms, the inner one builds one L_i as a running product.
Start each product at 1 and skip j == i, otherwise you divide by zero.
For each i: term = ys[i]; for each j != i: term *= (x - xs[j]) / (xs[i] - xs[j]); then total += term.
exercises.explanation: Five points of the sine curve reproduce sin(0.75) to three or four decimal places. The last value is the warning: outside the range of the points the polynomial follows its own shape, not the function's. With many equally spaced points the polynomial also swings wildly near the ends of the range, which is Runge's phenomenon; that is the reason for splines, which join low-degree pieces, and for Chebyshev points, which crowd toward the ends.

exercises.title: Back substitution
exercises.statement:
U is an upper triangular matrix, given as a list of rows: everything below the diagonal is zero, and nothing on the diagonal is. The last equation of U x = b therefore has one unknown, the one before it has two, and so on.

Write back_substitute(U, b). It returns the solution x as a list.
hints: Work from the last row up. When you reach row i, every x[j] with j > i is already known.
Row i says U[i][i] * x[i] + (the sum of U[i][j] * x[j] for j > i) = b[i].
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): compute s as that sum, then x[i] = (b[i] - s) / U[i][i].
exercises.explanation: This costs about n²/2 multiplications, against n³/3 for the elimination that produces the triangle. That gap is why LU factorisation pays: factor once, then each new right-hand side costs only two cheap triangular solves.

exercises.title: Gaussian elimination with pivoting
exercises.statement:
Write solve(A, b). A is a square matrix as a list of rows and b a list. Return the solution of A x = b as a list. Do not change A or b.

Use elimination with partial pivoting. For each column k in turn:

  1. Among rows k and below, find the one whose entry in column k is largest in absolute value, and swap it into row k.
  2. Subtract a multiple of row k from each row below it, chosen so that the row's entry in column k becomes zero. Do the same to b.

What is left is upper triangular. Finish with back substitution.

tests.test: print([round(v, 6) for v in solve([[2, 1], [1, 3]], [3, 5])], [round(v, 6) for v in solve([[0, 2], [1, 1]], [4, 3])])
print([round(v, 4) for v in solve([[1e-12, 1], [1, 1]], [1, 2])], [round(v, 6) for v in solve([[4]], [2])])

hints: Copy first: M = [row[:] for row in A] and y = b[:], then work on the copies.
The pivot row: p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][k])). Swap rows k and p in both M and y.
For each row r below k: factor = M[r][k] / M[k][k]; subtract factor * M[k][c] from M[r][c] for every column c from k, and factor * y[k] from y[r]. Then back substitution on M and y.
exercises.solution:
def solve(A, b):
    n = len(b)
    M = [row[:] for row in A]
    y = b[:]
    for k in range(n):
        p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][k]))
        M[k], M[p] = M[p], M[k]
        y[k], y[p] = y[p], y[k]
        for r in range(k + 1, n):
            factor = M[r][k] / M[k][k]
            for c in range(k, n):
                M[r][c] -= factor * M[k][c]
            y[r] -= factor * y[k]
    x = [0.0] * n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        s = sum(M[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))
        x[i] = (y[i] - s) / M[i][i]
    return x
exercises.explanation: The second system in the first test has a zero in the top-left corner, so elimination without a swap divides by zero. The last test is the subtler case: a pivot of 1e-12 is not zero, but dividing by it produces numbers so large that the other entries are rounded away, and the answer comes out as [0, 1]. Swapping the largest entry into the pivot position keeps every multiplier at most 1, which keeps the rounding under control.

exercises.title: LU factorisation
exercises.statement:
Write lu(A). A is a square matrix as a list of rows. Return two matrices (L, U) with L times U equal to A, where U is upper triangular and L is lower triangular with ones on its diagonal.

This is elimination with its multipliers kept. To clear column k of row r you subtract factor = U[r][k] / U[k][k] times row k. Store that factor in L[r][k]. Do not swap rows; the tests never need it. Do not change A.

tests.test:
A = [[4, -2, 1], [-2, 4, -2], [1, -2, 4]]
L, U = lu(A)
P = [[round(sum(L[i][k] * U[k][j] for k in range(3)), 9) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)]
print(P == A, [round(U[i][i], 4) for i in range(3)], L[0][1], U[2][0])

hints: Start with U as a copy of A with float entries, and L as the identity matrix.
The loops are the elimination loops: for each column k, for each row r below it.
factor = U[r][k] / U[k][k]; L[r][k] = factor; then U[r][c] -= factor * U[k][c] for every column c from k on.
exercises.explanation: Solving A x = b now takes two triangular solves: L y = b forwards, then U x = y backwards. The n³ work is done once, however many right-hand sides follow. The determinant comes free as the product of U's diagonal. A real library swaps rows as in the exercise before and returns the swaps too, as P A = L U. For a symmetric positive definite matrix the same idea gives the Cholesky factor, with half the work.

exercises.title: Jacobi iteration
exercises.statement:
For a large system, elimination can cost too much. An iterative method starts from a guess and improves it.

Jacobi's method solves equation i for x[i], using the previous guess for all the other unknowns:

new_x[i] = (b[i] - sum of A[i][j] * x[j] for j != i) / A[i][i]

Write jacobi(A, b, steps). Start from all zeros, do steps sweeps, and return the guess. Every value in a sweep is computed from the guess of the sweep before.

tests.test:
A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]
b = [1, 2]
print([round(v, 4) for v in jacobi(A, b, 1)], [round(v, 4) for v in jacobi(A, b, 2)], jacobi(A, b, 0))

hints: Keep two lists: x, the previous guess, and new_x, the one being built. Replace x only when the sweep is complete.
For each i, add up A[i][j] * x[j] over every j except i.
new_x = [(b[i] - sum(A[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(n) if j != i)) / A[i][i] for i in range(n)], then x = new_x.
exercises.explanation: Because each new value depends only on the previous sweep, all n updates of a sweep can run at once. Jacobi is the blur kernel again: two buffers, one launch per sweep. It converges when each diagonal entry outweighs the rest of its row, which is called diagonal dominance. The systems that come from heat flow and other differential equations have that property and are mostly zeros, which is where iterative methods beat elimination.

exercises.title: Gauss-Seidel iteration
exercises.statement:
Gauss-Seidel changes one thing in Jacobi's method: as soon as a new x[i] is computed it is used, in the same sweep, for the unknowns after it. There is one list, updated in place.

Write gauss_seidel(A, b, tol). Start from all zeros. After each sweep, look at the largest absolute change that any x[i] made in that sweep; stop when it is below tol. Return (x, sweeps): the solution and the number of sweeps done, counting the last one.

tests.test:
x, sweeps = gauss_seidel([[4, 1], [2, 3]], [1, 2], 1e-6)
print([round(v, 5) for v in x], sweeps)

A = [[10, -1, 2], [-1, 11, -1], [2, -1, 10]]
x, sweeps = gauss_seidel(A, [6, 25, -11], 1e-8)
print([round(v, 5) for v in x], sweeps)

hints: One list x. Inside a sweep, the sum for row i reads x[j] straight from that list, so it picks up the values already updated.
Track the largest change of the sweep: change = max(change, abs(new - x[i])) before you store new.
while True: do a sweep, add 1 to sweeps, and if change < tol: return x, sweeps.
exercises.explanation: Using the newest values roughly halves the number of sweeps Jacobi needs on these systems. The cost is that the sweep is now a chain: x[1] waits for x[0], so it cannot be shared out as it stands. Parallel versions colour the unknowns like a chessboard and update all of one colour at once. Successive over-relaxation, SOR, goes one step further: it moves each unknown past its Gauss-Seidel value by a factor ω between 1 and 2, x[i] += ω * (new - x[i]), and with a good ω converges far faster.

exercises.title: A chain after n steps
exercises.statement:
A Markov chain has states 0 to n - 1 and a transition matrix P, given as a list of rows: P[i][j] is the probability of moving to state j when in state i. Each row adds up to 1.

start[i] is the probability of beginning in state i. After one step, the probability of being in state j is the sum over i of start[i] * P[i][j].

Write after_steps(P, start, steps). It returns the list of probabilities after that many steps.

tests.test:
P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5]]
print([round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [1, 0], 1)], [round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [1, 0], 2)], after_steps(P, [1, 0], 0))

P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5]]
print([round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [1, 0], 50)], [round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [0, 1], 50)])

hints: One step is a new list of the same length. Entry j collects probability from every state i.
new[j] = sum(dist[i] * P[i][j] for i in range(n)).
Repeat that steps times, replacing dist with new each time, and return dist.
exercises.explanation: The distribution is a row vector multiplied by P on its right, once per step. The Chapman-Kolmogorov equations say the same thing for matrices: the n-step probabilities are the entries of P multiplied by itself n times. The last test starts in two different states and ends in the same place after 50 steps. The chain has forgotten where it began; the next exercise finds that limit directly.

exercises.title: The stationary distribution
exercises.statement:
A distribution pi is stationary for a chain when one more step leaves it unchanged: pi times P is pi again. For a chain that can get from every state to every other, and is not periodic, every start drifts toward it.

Write stationary(P, tol). Start from the even distribution, 1 / n in every state. Keep taking one step; stop when no entry changed by more than tol in the last step, and return the distribution.
hints: It is the step from the exercise before inside a while True: loop.
After computing new, measure max(abs(new[j] - dist[j]) for j in range(n)).
Replace dist with new first, then return it if that largest change is at most tol.
exercises.explanation: This is power iteration: multiply by the matrix until the vector stops moving. What it finds is the left eigenvector of P for eigenvalue 1. The second test is a birth and death chain, the kind behind queueing models, and its answer [0.25, 0.5, 0.25] can be checked by hand from the balance of flow between neighbours: 0.25 × 0.5 going up from state 0 equals 0.5 × 0.25 coming down from state 1. How fast the iteration settles is set by the second largest eigenvalue, which is the mixing time question from your data science course.

exercises.title: A single-server queue
exercises.statement:
Customers arrive at random at an average rate of lam per hour, and one server handles them at an average rate of mu per hour. This is the M/M/1 queue. When lam < mu it settles into a steady state with:

  • utilisation rho = lam / mu, the fraction of time the server is busy
  • L = rho / (1 - rho), the mean number in the system
  • Lq = rho * rho / (1 - rho), the mean number waiting, not counting the one being served
  • W = 1 / (mu - lam), the mean time in the system
  • Wq = rho / (mu - lam), the mean time spent waiting

Write mm1(lam, mu). It returns a dictionary with the keys "rho", "L", "Lq", "W" and "Wq". If lam is not less than mu the queue grows without limit: return None.

tests.test: print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in mm1(2, 3).items()})
print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in mm1(9, 10).items()}, mm1(3, 3), mm1(5, 4))

hints: Check the unstable case first and return None.
Compute rho once and use it in the other formulas.
Build the dictionary with the five keys spelled exactly as in the statement.
exercises.explanation: The last test is why this model matters outside an exam. A server that can handle 10 requests an hour answers in 12 minutes at half load, an hour at 90%, and ten hours at 99%. Delay does not rise in proportion to load; it explodes as utilisation nears 1. That is the reason a model server is sized to run well below full use. The formulas obey Little's law, L = lam * W, which holds for any queue in steady state, not only this one.

exercises.title: PageRank
exercises.statement:
links[i] is the list of pages that page i links to. Pages are numbered 0 to n - 1.

A surfer on page i follows one of its links, chosen evenly, with probability d. Otherwise the surfer jumps to one of the n pages chosen evenly. A page with no links at all always jumps to a page chosen evenly.

Write pagerank(links, d, steps). Start with rank 1 / n on every page and apply this update steps times:

new[j] = (1 - d) / n + d * (sum of rank[i] / len(links[i]) over the pages i that link to j) + d * (total rank of the pages with no links) / n

Return the list of ranks.

tests.test:
r = pagerank([[1, 2], [2], [0]], 0.85, 60)
print([round(v, 4) for v in r], round(sum(r), 6))

r = pagerank([[1], []], 0.85, 80)
print([round(v, 4) for v in r], round(sum(r), 6), pagerank([[1], [0]], 0.5, 0))

hints: Each update builds a new list. Start every entry at (1 - d) / n plus the share from the pages without links, which is the same for every page.
Then push rank along the links: for each page i with links, each page j it links to receives d * rank[i] / len(links[i]).
dangling = sum(rank[i] for i in range(n) if not links[i]); new = [(1 - d) / n + d * dangling / n] * n; then the loop over links adds to new[j].
exercises.explanation: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk on the web graph, found by the power iteration of the exercise before. The random jump is what makes the chain able to reach every state, so that a single stationary distribution exists. Pushing rank along the links, instead of building an n by n matrix, is a sparse matrix-vector product: the work is proportional to the number of links. It is also the textbook MapReduce job, with one map and one reduce per update.

exercises.title: The best-fit direction
exercises.statement:
The rows of A are points in space. The direction along which they spread the most is the first right singular vector of A: the unit vector v that makes the length of A v as large as possible. That largest length is the first singular value.

Power iteration finds it. Start with v as the vector of all ones, scaled to length 1. Then repeat steps times: compute w = A v, then u = Aᵀ w (multiply by A, then by its transpose), and replace v with u scaled to length 1.

Write top_singular(A, steps). A is a list of rows. Return (sigma, v): the length of A v for the final v, and that v as a list.

tests.test:
s, v = top_singular([[3, 0], [0, 1]], 30)
print(round(s, 4), [round(x, 4) for x in v])
